text: Let me start of by saying this. If you want the short version review, skip to the last part (gameplay), otherwise enjoy my thorough review of the game.  The first steps: If you are totally new to survival crafting games, you will be utterly lost in this game. When you start out, you don’t have any tutorial to walk you through the game, and it most certainly doesn’t hold your hand in any way. You have to figure out stuff by picking, chopping, looting, killing and crafting stuff along the way.   User interface: The UI is very easy to use. Not much to say here, even a total noob can figure this out.  Moving about: This game gives you wings! You can travel over land very fast in this game if you make use of your glider and strategic spires and hills. Otherwise you will have quite the adventure tracking over lands and channelling your inner mountain goat.  Combat: The combat is in it’s way very simplistic and there are no combo’s or funny buttons and special skills. It’s just straight forward stabbing, slicing and shooting. That said, it is very enjoyable to just go into a stabbing frenzy when you duel wield (like I do, hehehe).  Skills: It does have a skill tree where you do branch of into your three major groups: tanky, healy and damagy. And it also offers stamina and magic skills alike. It’s a fairy small-med sized skill tree, and doesn’t need any special builds or manuals to be optimum in any way. Players are free to build as they want.  Survival: Food is a bonus to have, but not as a means to keep you from starving. There is no dying in here when you don’t find food, or having a grumpy character when you’re not eating a balanced diet. The foods boost your character stats and are helpful in surviving the great outdoors.  Farming: Yes, there is absolutely farming in this game. If you’d like to grow your own ingredients you can easily do so, with hardly any limits, except time. Patience with farming is extremely rewarding. Where some things will be ready for harvesting in a day or so, it is best to leave others to grow for a while to better reap the benefits.  Building: I’ll say this. If you love building in games where you have no limits, you’ll have a blast in here. It does offer a wide selection of building materials and furnishings with no caps and restrictions, so long as you build within your flame radius. It could however use a bit of a fine tweaking tool and more rotation options for blocks, but other than that, it is thoroughly enjoyable to build masterpieces in this game.  Scenery: There are some very, very beautiful and well thought out places in this game. Even though it does have some re-use over some building exteriors, like the spires, there are equally places that are very unique and you can immediately feel the love and effort that was put in to create some of these spaces (e.g. a beautiful woodland cave when you’re heading to the tar swamp)  Gameplay: After playing this game for some time, I found it to be very enjoyable (especially if you play with someone else who also enjoys it). There is a lot to do in this game if you love questing, building, farming, and being stared at by fellow survivors as you contemplate life choices. It does have some grinding for resources, but not to the point of having to have a second life for it. It does have some game issues here and there where it will randomly crash and feel a bit annoying to redo some events, and it does have a slight lag at some spots. That said, myself and my hubby found this game to be awesome and we easily reach for it to play together. If you like Valheim, you will probably enjoy this game a lot too.  Hope this helps all future peeps who are still deciding on whether to buy this game. I think that it well deserving of trying out, and definitely worth the money.

Even though it does have some re-use over some building exteriors, like the spires, there are equally places that are very unique and you can immediately feel the love and effort that was put in to create some of these spaces (e.g. a beautiful woodland cave when you’re heading to the tar swamp)  Gameplay: After playing this game for some time, I found it to be very enjoyable (especially if you play with someone else who also enjoys it). There is a lot to do in this game if you love questing, building, farming, and being stared at by fellow survivors as you contemplate life choices. It does have some grinding for resources, but not to the point of having to have a second life for it. It does have some game issues here and there where it will randomly crash and feel a bit annoying to redo some events, and it does have a slight lag at some spots. That said, myself and my hubby found this game to be awesome and we easily reach for it to play together. If you like Valheim, you will probably enjoy this game a lot too.  Hope this helps all future peeps who are still deciding on whether to buy this game. I think that it well deserving of trying out, and definitely worth the money.

text: Enshrouded is what happens when survival crafting games finally decide to respect your time and your imagination.  You start out thinking, “Alright, another ‘punch trees, eat berries, don’t die’ situation.” Three hours later you’re architect of a small kingdom, casually terraforming hillsides, building a house that would make medieval Pinterest jealous, and wondering why every other game suddenly feels… mehh  The world? Gorgeous and haunting. The shroud mechanic? Actually tense instead of annoying. Combat? Solid enough to keep you honest and it involves skill. But the real star is the building system, it’s really good. “I’ll just place one wall” turns into “why is it 2AM and I’m handcrafting a spiral staircase in this useless tower I just built using scaffolding like a skyscraper builder in Bangkok ??!”  Also, co-op is where this game quietly becomes elite-tier. Nothing like you and your longtime gaming buddies shrieking like little girls because a one-eyed monster suddenly emerges from a dark corner and starts to eat you.  Is it perfect? I actually think so. For me it's THE game of 2026 ( yes, I was late to the hypetrain )  Verdict: If Valheim and Zelda had a child that went to architecture school, this would be it.  10/10, no doubt

text: Extremely addictive experience with casual elements of survival while being visually pleasing, it's a great start to early access. Co-op experience has been 10/10. You can have your own solo world and private experience by yourself, then take that same character to a brand new server to experience the fun with friends without affecting your save.  When playing with friends, if a quest is completed while you're offline you will still have the quest marker on your map and the quest items/bosses respawn! You can still go to the marker and "complete" the quest which will remove it from your quest log and give you XP.   There's a huge variety of side quests sprinkled throughout the map through Lore books, some are given to you by the NPCs in your base. They're entirely optional obviously but they do help you explore the cursed lands of Embervale. What makes this even better is that side quests are repeatable, so if you have a shared server, people who miss these can go back to grab them at any time or complete them while they wait for the rest of the party to progress together.     They chased elixirs and released the Shroud.   It is time to ignite your spark, Flameborn.

text: This is a pretty amazing, open sandbox game, with a lot to explore and do. The graphics are beautiful, and the fact that one can modify almost anything in the game leaves a lot of room for creativity.  I am giving the game a negative rating because the gearing system in the game pretty much ruins everything else.   This is a survival crafting game, but Keen Games has decided to give loot the RNG loot box treatment instead of the tried and true gather new resource craft better equipment of other survival crafters... Even Dune Awakening does this better!  The loot in this game has quality tiers. Players CAN craft equipment up to Rare tier, but it is almost always MUCH worse than what one will get out of chests.   Why is this a problem? Well, during EA players figured out that one could build a base near a chest and then log off and reboot their game to reset the chest thus shortening the tedious loot grind.  To "fix" this, Keen Games made chests have a 1 hour PLAY TIME cooldown before refreshing. But it gets better! It is a 1 hour playtime IN A SEPARATE ZONE cooldown. This means that once one is done running around a zone, looting every chest that they know about, one has to LEAVE said zone for an hour. Zones are broken into level ranges, this essentially means that a player needs to leave the content zone that they are currently leveled up to and go to a previous zone for an hour if they want to try for better loot...   Then there are the changes to the Hallow Halls. Class specific loot chests have been added to the end of these 1-2 hour long dungeons that fit warrior/ranger/wizard builds, BUT the chest spawns are random. For example, I spent an hour running through the Kindle Wastes Hallow Hall as a wizard character only to have two ranger weapon gold chests and a warrior armor gold chest spawn. Out of the 5 silver chests that spawned, only two where wizard weapon chests. NONE were wizard armor chests.  This means that if I want level 27-32 gold quality wizard armor I now have to wait 30min to an hour OF PLAY TIME for the hall to reset AND TRY AGAIN!  As long as Enshroud maintains this ridiculously time wasting loot system I can't recommend it. Every other good thing in the game is overshadowed by the fact that one will out level their gear and then get gear checked by high level mobs while trying to explore leading one to have to go back and tediously try to RNG to better loot.  Did I mention that hallow halls are tuned for 4 player teams and do not scale to solo runs? Because fighting two undead cyclops and two waves of Hallow all while having to kite or be chain staggered to death is super fun.   PS: There is no "end game" to  Enshrouded, so just blitzing to max level to simplify the farm is pointless and will ruin what there is to actually enjoy about the game. There are custom settings where one can just nerf enemies into the ground and not worry about gear at all if one wants to focus on exploration and lore, but I feel NEEDING to do that to not have to gear farm just to keep up with enemies is just poor game design.   Recommendation to fix the issue: Give players the ability to upgrade equipment continuously, and give us the ability to raise quality tier via crafting. To prevent people from over leveling their equipment to an absurd degree add in additional tiers of runes similar to how we upgrade gems.

text: Don't let the Early Access state fool you or put you off: this is an absolute standout of a game that deserves so much more recognition, Enshrouded is a love letter of a game to the open world survival craft genre. Every feature that you could want, that you would usually need mods for with other games, is already built in.   Craft from containers? Included. Free placement or snap to grid? Already there. Vanity armor system? Present and being constantly upgraded (hello brand new tinting station!) NPCs that can set to wander or stay in place? Done. Tamed creatures you can pet? Absolutely, and you even get a cute buff. Enshrouded is a game made by developers who love and have extensively played this genre before, and it shows.   And the BUILDING SYSTEM allows some of the most gorgeous, creative, freedom allowing games I've ever seen. The voxel building mean your not limited to pre-existing shapes and structures. Make sure you have the "Voxel Detail Models" in your Display settings turned on to at least Balanced, if your computer will allow. Quality if you want to be blown away by the gorgeous detail of each building block.  This game is extremely friendly to players who are new to the survival crafting genre. If you struggle in open world sandboxes to find something to do, the questing system here rewards exploration and progression without being too linear with many side quests, NPC fetch quests, cosmetic item sets to find and collect, etc.  Even though it's an Early Access title (and you would never know it based on the game state) this is an extremely well-developed and supported game. Devs are prompt, responsive, open to feedback from the community, and very active with big updates and quick hotfixes. Everything you could want.  It's not an exaggeration to say that once this game hits full release, it's going to be a gaming milestone. Cheers to Enshrouded!

text: Enshrouded feels like a game I should love, but I find myself bored and slogging through it just to finish the content there is. I haven't made it to the desert or the new mountain area yet, and it's still EA, so maybe some of this will change.  Cons: -There are only a handful of different enemy types that get reused through the entire game. This is a big map and you'll come across the same 4 bandits (5 if you count the dogs, 6 if you count the bosses) everywhere. -Combat is essentially spam left click and dodge sometimes. No abilities, no cooldowns, no skill involved whatsoever. -The item progression feels terrible. You don't craft weapons, you find them. You do craft different armors, but they never felt like a true upgrade over the random pieces you find. -The building system is probably great if you're a creative person, but for me, it felt extremely unintuitive and clunky. -Optimization is terrible. The game itself runs ok, but when I open the map and zoom out, I can literally hear my GPU shit itself and my fps drops to 3 (you read that right, three). This has been a complaint by a lot of people with much better PCs than me since the game released (just google the issue and you'll see dozens of threads on Steam and Reddit about it). A year with such a glaring issue? That seems like a huge red flag for me.  Pros: -I really like how every piece of lore puts a new map marker or starts a new quest. Gives me a reason to check everything, and there is a lot to check. -In theory, I do like the creativity that building allows you. You can put a new base almost anywhere. You like the way the ruins of that city that you just cleared of enemies looks? Well now you can make your own neighborhood in the middle of it using whatever houses remain. That random tower looks cool? Well, now it's your random tower. -Voxel based terrain alteration. The real stuff, not the "my pickaxe just makes a dent in the ground." You can tunnel through a mountain and build a village in the middle of it. You can dig a hole 80m deep and build a house down there like some thriftstore dwarf.

text: Here's the thing- I used to love this game. It was/is really good and fun to play when it flows right. It's just gotten to the point where you're questlocked by everything to do or accomplish anything. A typical gameplay session goes like this for us anymore: log in, pick a quest to do or some kind of objective you want to complete, start out doing that thing, and then find out "Oh, I need to do this other thing first, oh but wait I have to do another thing before I can do that, dang it I got halfway through THAT thing and I can't go any farther until I upgrade my shroud passage, but wait I can't do that until I get this thing, but I have to complete this before I do that" and alllllll of that is because you want to like LITERALLY make a SANDWICH. It's turned into a bunch of running around to end up frustrated and feeling like you didn't accomplish anything. I'm really bummed to post this because again I love the game and the concept and the combat and  the building system and all of it, but it's just too many quests to keep up with and very little indication of  what order to complete things in or if you will not be able to complete something that you've got active. I would love to play again if they can find a way to help players prioritize or something, but for now it's just too frustrating to play.

text: Yet another game where you pick up sticks and rocks so that you can make better sticks and rocks to get better-better stick-rock-things and build things. Someday, one of these games will let me build all the way from stick-rock to spaceflight, but this isn't that game. text: My honest Enshrouded review. It is mixed feel free to tell me if you think i am wrong.  Okay so lets start with the good things. I do not write reviews unless i have put in at least 100 hours into a survival game. The building in this game is far more superior than any survival game i have ever played. Better than Ark, Atlas, Space engineers, Empyrion, Valheim, Nightingale and the forest. It is absolutely mind blowing. I will add some pictures of some of the bad ass houses i made. Single block placement and voxel based environments are outstanding. My only gripe on this subject is there is no rounded or triangle piece blocks. Which is sad because the building is phenomenal. Hopefully that will be added in the future. The other issue i have is why do you have chairs and benches and stuff when you cant even sit on them. Every survival game i have ever played has a sitting mechanic even the worst ones. Beautiful chairs with no ass to sit on lol.  I think the movement is fun i love the glider and grapple. Combat can be pretty fun at times could use a little more different types of combat moves for different weapons. Everything feels somewhat the same at the current stage.  Progression feels good but its so fast i literally beat the entire game in 30 hours with one friend. That is way to dam fast to be considered a survival game even in early access. How you have these different tier levels but bronze didn't even feel worth my time just went straight into iron. also why make a giant map that we can only explore a third of it. I understand its early access but it felt sad to me to know i could go there but you wont let me,.  In my opinion the survival mechanics are pointless. You do not need to eat or rest just make a warrior build throw on health regen pants and your good. Never need to eat or make food again. The game feels much more like Skyrim with building except there is no dragons. Could use more creature or different enemy's.  All and all is it not really a survival game. More of a RPG with building which i dont hate that. Just wish the RPG aspects had a lot more to offer. If you don't have much of a end game or longevity to offer the players probably should have come out with PVP like ark did. Ark was ass when it first came out but i played 1000s of hours in that game 7000 to be exact. For this game the only reason ill be getting back on it is for the building aspects because there so good. Once you get to iron armor what else is there to do. Its not super dynamic to run another play through. Maybe make it a little more grindy so it keeps players invested for longer than 30 hours.  I would only recommend this game for just how solid the building mechanics are. Also for someone just wanting a good 30 to 50 hours of fun. I got more playtime from valheim going from copper to silver tier weapons than i did from this entire game. it took me 300 hours to solo valheim that is with building big ass houses. i Spent 50 hours on this game just building one house that to me was worth more time than actually beating the game.  I do look forward to seeing what the game will do and the updates. i don't really care for graphics on games or other things for me its the content is the most important above all else. Empyrion is one ugly looking game but with all its content 500 hours was easy to invest. I still never beat it even with that many hours i want to be invested in your world. Survival games are about committing to live in a realm and surviving in it. This game has not hit that mark yet.

text: 10hrs in and I must say, this has the potential to be one of the best survival games of all time. In its current state, I would recommend this game for anyone who enjoys single player adventure survival games. The multiplayer aspect is mid, at best.   The game uses a shared progression system which means if you are playing with friends, you’ll have to all play at the exact same time or risk missing out on quests, XP and skill points. Unfortunately for me, my friends who are interested in this game won’t play it because we have mostly different schedules. Which sucks, because I love playing these games with friends.  The game, overall, is incredibly fun. The combat is well thought out, and it doesn’t have an overly complicated stats system. The food/water buffs are easy to understand. The building is what sets this game apart, however. There seems to be plenty of materials to build with, and the voxel based building is insane. A highlight is the fact you can build onto existing structures found in the world with ease. Renovations galore.  There are a few things I wish this game would change.  1. Let us build on diagonals. Everything is set to 90° angles which limits creative expression. Probably the biggest let down for me. 2. Get rid of shared progression. 3. Let us have pets, mounts and farm animals rather than going into the wilds to find food. I want to build a homestead. 4. Give us difficulty settings, and ways to tailor the gameplay to our own liking.

text: This is the best game I’ve ever played, full stop. Almost 1000 hours in, and I still log in “just to do one thing” and end up six objectives deep, forgetting what I even came for.  From the moment you step into its massive, detailed world, Enshrouded gives you endless reasons to keep exploring. The Shroud zones are dangerous in the best way — not just because of the enemies, but because they pull you in with the promise of loot, hidden areas, and challenges that turn a quick trip into a long adventure. Every journey seems to create new goals on the fly, whether it’s uncovering a chest tucked deep in a dungeon, unlocking a new recipe, or stumbling onto the perfect spot for a future build.  And building in Enshrouded isn’t just a side activity — it’s one of the game’s greatest strengths. The system is incredibly flexible, letting you shape anything from a simple shelter to a sprawling fortress without fighting the controls. Voxel-based terrain shaping means the land itself becomes part of your design, allowing you to carve cliffs, level ground, or embed structures into mountainsides. With plenty of materials to gather and a wide variety of blocks, furniture, and decorations, every base feels unique and personal.  When I’m not building, I’m chasing something — scouring for loot, hunting bosses, or fine-tuning my gear to squeeze out just a little more performance. The game constantly tempts me forward: one more upgrade, one more dungeon, one more reason to push deeper into the mist.  Some players say there’s “nothing to do” here. Maybe at some point. In nearly 1000 hours, I’ve never run out of goals. The freedom to follow whatever catches my attention — whether it’s combat, crafting, exploration, or construction — has kept me hooked longer than almost any other game I’ve played.  - Final Verdict: 1000/10. This isn’t just a game you finish — it’s a world you live in, and one you’ll keep coming back to.

text: This game is soooo close to being there.   Pros: - Excellent building system - Crafting feels intuitive - Open world exploration feels good - Some of the best opening hours of a survival crafter I have experienced - Major boss fights feel cool  Cons: - This game is poorly optimized - The combat starts off feeling good but by mid-game it starts to feel very repetitive  - Enemy models do not change, some new enemies get introduced as you progress further but there is still very little diversity among enemy models - The generic boss fights are also duplicated quite a bit  The number one issue preventing me from recommending this game is the poor optimization. The combat system along with enemy variety could also use work If you are more into the building and crafting aspect of this game, it is great! There is a mysterious world to explore and I am usually a sucker for that. Just a couple things holding this game back from greatness in my opinion.

text: Enshrouded might not be perfect, but its the closest game I've played to it. this game has almost everything i want in many games genres all wrapped into one, so this is a personal perfection, almost every itch scratched, if i were a dog my leg would be kicking ;-).  I rarely write a review good or bad, and very rarely as long and lengthy as this one, but this game is an obsession, and its not even fully released.  Map Huge open beautiful world, and by huge i mean huge, im aprox 170+ hrs into the game, and my map might be about 60% explored. its not empty miles with endless running from point to point just to have a huge map. Because of Lore!  Lore Enshrouded is jam packed with Lore, if its your thing. If its your thing, read everything and get a story of why the world is the way it is, or don't, but its everywhere for the reading. I personally don't like meaningless rambling NPC chatter, I'm glad the developers chose the method of story telling, with a limited amount of NPC chatter.  Loot At first appearance it seems like what loot? they don't give you anything, you earn it, but once you get some clothes and armor going and start exploring, its a never ending search and quest for bigger and greater pieces of armor and weapons, some you craft some you find as quests. there is armor and then there is the option for appearance which allows both armor and cosmetic only, so if i want to look like a rogue and wear heavy armor since i play a warrior, I can. it has a lot of armor, from magic user, rogue, warrior, to all the subclasses in-between, there is also a plethora of NPC type gear, so if I'm in the mood to look like a grave digger (actual set) i can.When i say a lot of armor, i dont mean, chain mail with 20 different names and stat buffs, all using the same visual set of chain mail, Diablo is famous for.  no, im talking looking different, complete design difference, color, folds, spikes etc.   thats a big factor for me, I love looking at my armor, so I have a museum..... more in base building  Base Building Its not just a Conan or Valheim base builder, i mention both games cause i liked building sprawling basses in both. the building blocks and building system has improved on both. What makes it different is, true terraforming, talking Minecraft ability of truly digging down, building up, and building on in or under. This is a big thing, and really lets your imagination explode, don't believe me, they have the option were you can visit other peoples worlds and see, their creations. A group have built two spectacular builds, Rivendale and the Shire, OMFG, im talking truly amazing, movie set quality, every bit as accurate as i could see based on the books, games and movies. I have a museum, nothing grand, but for me, was a labor of love, its packed with about 50 complete armor sets on mannequins and enough partial sets still in a chest waiting to be displayed. I've not started the weapons wing, but its just as impressive collection of weapons, though I only keep the weapons with the cool factor, i search for and collect all armor sets.  Crafting, I'm not sure I've seen a game with the amount of crafting materials, as Enshrouded, which can be awesome and overwhelming at the same time, they did it smartly each area presents new and or new alternatives of previous areas. So you collection of materials and ways to store and manage it grow with you as you reach out into new regions. I use the word alternatives, because most recipes give you the ability to use the likewise material in place of the original. Charcoal as an example, say charcoal, uses wood and dirt to make, I can use Bamboo from end game areas instead of wood from the area i started in, same with the dirt, i can use sand from the desert if i have more. I used Bamboo because i have a beautiful Bamboo farm, and it produces a lot of wood, yes i mentioned Farming, a giant garden with everything from food to Alchemical plants. A ranch, with animals I've befriended and stable, for their products or Kull for food.  I mentioned end game Bamboo, yet only explored 60% of the game, its a true open world, not a linier game claiming its open, by unscalable walls and mountains, though Shrouds do hinder your travels they do not stop you from circumventing you. This is were the terraforming is such a huge factor for me. A steep unclimbable mountain, i dig, and build a cliff side stair way, though you can not build unless your withing a flame alter  area, which you can pop down almost anywhere you are limited by how many you can place which grows as you lvl. so i get my pick axe out and scaled a mountain and explored other areas, usually leading to me running for my life and laughing along the way, and collecting what I can.   Parkour, puzzles, hidden rooms, and gliders, very Zelda like experience, but in a darker world. for as big as the open world is, it doesn't lack in dungeons with different types, that are deep and vast. the Dungeon instances are a big and deep as the world is vast, some are puzzles and parkour others its a slaughter fest, and the Hollows well come leveled or bring friends.  Last comment, the difficulty options are nice, its not just an easy as intended normal or hard setting but you can go in and customize each area to your liking, make it easier then easy or harder then hard, adjust to were you find your happy. i dabbled with a side char, for a bit, i turned down the enemies str and hp, including bosses, but i turned up the amount that populate and turned up their agro, so while the enemies are weaker, getting attacked is more akin to diablo, instead of 3 wolves attacking its 7, or 10 skeletons its 50. it was fun, after release in a few months i might revisit that setting for a different exp, on a second play thru, if when i actually finish this char.   there is so much more, ive left a lot out, because its a fine line describing the game with out giving any spoilers. while many games have come before, nothing is truly new, its just they took the best of about 5 different genres and vastly improved on all of them, and seamlessly incorporated them all into one game and world. I have days i want to build, others explore, i can get my bloodlust adrenaline pumping action desires fulfilled, then farm, and craft.   the only negative, and it doesn't affect me, because my alien gaming laptop, but is a comment by others i cant refute, it is hardware demanding, as much as i want to recommend it to my own younger brother, he doesn't have the gaming rig i do, wives and kids come first.

text: I have such a love/hate relationship with this game. On one hand it achieves almost everything it sets out to do but at the same time I feel it's lacking. Looking past my frustrations with the sometimes buggy nature of the combat and the ball-torturing amount of enemies, this game has a lot of soul and a lot of good mechanics to play around with. So often I find myself wishing the world didn't feel so dead. That the NPC's I save and build homes for did more than just say "hey" at you in an obvious AI voice. I wish I could create settlements that feel alive. I wish I could create resource-links between settlements and interact with the world I am rebuilding. Features like that would set this game far above many others. Either way it's a great game with a fun progression loop and a very engaging building system.

text: I really wanted to like this game, and I've tried to play it a few times. Restarted when 1.0 hit of course. It does have a certain appeal from the outside. But once I am in I don't seem to get it. The world certainly looks cool, but it doesn't feel alive. I don't know why I am there. Why am I going to all these places? I need an incentive, but where is it? Everything I find in this world feels the same. I know it's a carefully crafted world, and maybe that is part of the problem: It doesn't convince me it's actually a world.  These weird NPC's I have to rescue, and then summon with the special wand, who then just unconvincingly and endlessly wander around the house, repeating the same things over and over again. I don't enjoy the noises they constantly make either.   I don't enjoy the building system. I don't enjoy having to build a house. And this is coming from someone who really loves building in games such as Valheim.  Then there's the actual shroud. A miserable place, and I hate being there. I understand this is by design of course... But I find it depressing. I loathe having to go there, and I don't like the time limit I have either. Creatures hidden in the darkness, irritating bugs spawning. If I could avoid the shroud, I would.  Combat always feels clunky to me. When done right, movement and combat feel convincing. Many games out there succeed very well at doing that. But in this game I feel the character often seems to slide, especially when strafing. They seem to be on rails, like they're not really there, but on a green screen. I get that it takes some getting used to, and you get better at how the game works. But I never enjoy it.  The visuals are unique, for sure, but do feel like an odd blend of Fable and Elder Scrolls. It's an odd blend of cartoonish and realistic, and I just don't enjoy that kind of aesthetic.  Then there is the music: It's not bad music, but it feels off to me in the world of Enshrouded. If I were to be blunt: It's dull, it's boring, and rather repetitive. It doesn't compliment or even drive the world. I could give examples, but I'd rather not as I understand this is rather subjective. Sound effects also don't really land for me. Where's the 'umph' , if you know what I mean? Voiceover work is decent I'd say, but you can tell that for all of the stories/letters you find someone sat down and read them all as if it was an e-book, not a game.  I don't know. Maybe I simply don't like the game, and that's that. But I do keep coming back, and wish it was something I'd enjoy more. I'll give the game a fair chance, and play some more. Maybe I'll change my mind and revisit this review.  As odd as it may be after my rant, I do want to recommend this game as I do feel it offers a lot that people should give a chance. I did enjoy myself to a degree.

text: To celebrate 1000 hours in the game I decided to recommend officially. It's a perfect family coop. We came to it from Valheim after we hit 1800 hours and got tired of Mistland. Enshrouded feels much more balanced and the voxel based world is an amazing experience. It's beautifully and efficiently implemented and opens crazy opportunities, like digging your way through a rock just because. 1.0 is coming next month and we are looking forward to the new biomes and new toys. It's fun. Sometimes tedious but very rewarding fun. Sorry Valheim, we are not coming back.

text: Honestly? 9/10. $30 for this game is fucking insane to me, it's well worth more. Tldr below.   Edit: Update to review - it's been mentioned that my complaint written further below was unjustifed regarding Townsfolk. Fact is I hadn't made it far enough to experience the full potential of the Nov 2024 update. There is so much content I just hadn't made it far enough to see it, and now I can happily say they delivered. 10/10. Play the damn game folks. They are STILL building on this thing in 2025.  Enshrouded is incredible. Gameplay reminds me of Fable, the 2024 edition, but with crafting. Coming from Valheim and Medieval/Sengoku Dynasty - games I enjoyed but never felt true "satisfaction" (always felt like something was missing or overly complex) - Enshrouded checks boxes. Nearly all of them.   Enshrouded in its initial release form was *Good*. Now, it is *powerfully* good. I am a survival crafting noob, I dont buy into hardcore survival sims that require extensive wiki's and google docs to figure out basic recipes and how to avoid starvation. Enshrouded figured itself out, the formula just works whether you're hardcore or casual.   With the recent additions in November 2024, adding an insanely MASSIVE zone to the already massive map and QOL updates as well as aesthetic bonuses, the only thing selling this game short is its lack of Medieval Dynasty's town NPC population and lack of guidance regarding how to acquire some recipes. There are numerous difficulty options to cater your experience towards combat focused or crafting focused. Venture into a cave and only face 1 or 2 enemies (or none at all) - or dial it up and face 50 with extra health/dmg/etc.  Finish your first adventure, return home and build the ugliest or coziest mansion on a giant property of your choice. I opted to increase gathering yield so I can hop into building faster, with slightly harder enemies in higher counts - it's perfect. You can build and craft *anywhere* - and the intuitive creative nature of the building system is top notch. Items meld and morph into each other, creating new shapes and structures you couldn't do by default. The game encourages experimentation, build a Lord of the Rings castle or an old school Japanese mansion or both. Among *many many many* other styles.   The combat is simple enough, but more in depth than Valheim by far. The skill tree is a simplified version of PoE. Battlemage, Tank, Ranger, Paladin, among many other styles.   It also has the potential to play on a potato based on my past experience with the initial release version. I've since upgraded and the game is gorgeous at max quality. I just sat atop a mountain and played music for half an hour for no reason at all than the satisfying aesthetic.   My complaint: home bases feel slightly too empty. Many of us were looking forward to the "Townsfolk" update, assuming we would be able to populate our home bases with commoners/villagers etc. It's the reason I initially quit. I loved crafting and fighting, but I felt alone. Then the Nov 2024 update for Townsfolk turned out to be just an addition to the *crafter* NPCs you can place in your base. Unlike Medieval/Sengoku Dynasty, where your village can have 50+ commoners roaming about, doing jobs, hanging out, etc.  Tldr: Beautiful game, insane amount of content, express your inner adventurer or crafter. Devs care. 10x better than it was at release. Home bases still feel a little lonely, Townsfolk update wasn't what many of us expected. Still, more than worth the price, I wouldve gladly paid $60+.

text: I have played for about 800 hrs. The story is interesting, and the game is definitely playable solo. I completed the game, through level 35 as a solo player with out much problem. Some things take longer (i.e. Hollow Halls), but nothing is impossible to complete. The group play is pretty good too, though there are currently performance issue, though not surprising since this in in EA. There is also no in-game chat (text or voice), but I found a group of people, and we were able to overcome it using Discord. Used basic building blocks in-game to write out Discord info.  I absolutely love the building system. Though it could use work with camera control and additional options (round shapes), the building potential is endless. Of my almost 800 hrs of play, at least 600 has been spent building.  I highly recommend this game for anyone who likes survival/building games!

text: Unfortunately, this game is not enjoyable for me as a solo player.  Walking long distances to prominent landmarks makes the world feel very empty to me.  The progression system seems forced and very linear.  Crafting only progresses a little, as quest progression frequently caps you out.  Worst of all, exploration as a solo player feels very unrewarding. After running around and looting through multiple landmarks, there is often not a single thing of value.  The loot is almost always outdated, under-leveled, or for the wrong specialization, failing to provide rewarding items and experience.  Overall, it is a very fad experience that I won't recommend to any solo player.

text: I've been stuck in Fallout 76 for years—mostly because of the base-building system—yeah… I'm a sucker for that. In 2024, for Christmas, my best friend asks me, [i]"What do you want as a gift?" "I don't know, bro, the games in my wishlist are ranked by preference."[/i] And what does the idiot do? He buys me a game he liked, which WASN’T EVEN IN MY WISHLIST. In fact, I wasn't even interested when he first pitched it to me so we could play together. Oh well… 110 hours later, I can confidently say: [b]it sucks. Don’t play it with friends. It doesn’t have good graphics. It doesn’t have new mechanics. It doesn’t have an awesome base-building system. It doesn’t have tons of cool biomes to explore. It doesn’t have constant updates. It doesn’t have insanely smooth gameplay similar to Breath of the Wild. It doesn’t have cool stuff to discover at every step.[/b] Oh, how I wish all of this weren’t outright lies and the reality wasn’t the complete opposite. [h3]OK FINE, ALEX, IT’S ONE OF THE COOLEST GAMES I’VE PLAYED LATELY, AND IT HOOKED ME JUST AS MUCH AS 76, Terraria, AND OTHER INSANELY GOOD GAMES THAT ARE WORTH EVERY PENNY—AND THAT PUT MANY TRIPLE-A TITLES TO SHAME.[/h3] Happy now? Now get in Enshrouded and give me that wand — I respecced, and I’m a mage now.

text: Well, I told myself I'd review the game at 100 hours. 99.9 works too! (Early Access)  Let me start by saying this is the most fun I've had on a game in YEARS!  Think, Skyrim, Valheim, Breath of the Wild, Minecraft, and The Forest combined. No cannibals, just spooky moments.  The Positives:  1. Co-op makes this game incredible! I can't tell you how much fun it is to play with someone who will read the lore with you in goofy voices, jump off cliffs with you randomly, and abandon you in the middle of a boss fight because they almost got one shot. Having a loot goblin friend makes it even better. 2.It's GORGEOUS!! Seriously, I can't emphasize how beautiful this game is! I run a 2080ti and I find myself on top of mountains and trees admiring the views from above or along the water admiring the reflection of the sunset more often than I play the game. OH, and the rain! The change in sound the ground makes when its wet or dry, the way it sounds inside compared to outside, and how it looks at sunset is phenomenal! 3. The game runs incredibly smooth! From fighting hordes of enemies, to jumping into a pool of water, and even how it feels to jump off of a spire and dive straight down while gliding.  4. Farming! If you enjoy comfy cozy games like I do or you have a friend or partner who isn't combat oriented but loves to farm and decorate. Then this game is for you. I've spent a solid 10-15 hours so far (with many more to come) just designing our homes, barn, castle (Fort Kelvin in my case) and I still have more to do. 5. Crafting - Yes the farming is included in this but I want to say that this is the best crafting I've ever used in a game. It may not be as complex as minecraft with their redstone but the way you can combine and design using the voxel game system is amazing. You can create a base completely from scratch or even take over existing areas and build off of them. I HIGHLY recommend Fort Kelvin after you unlock Hannah Reed from her quest because you can rebuild the walls, buildings, and the cave system to have a nice clean fort that keeps all of your villagers in a safe area.  6. VOXEL GAME - This brings me to my next point. You can literally destroy 99% of the areas/buildings/trees etc. There are obviously specific things that can't but this opens up ways to get around the world because of it. Can't get past a gate early game and don't have a grapple? Mine around it. Can't get into a tower because brand new? Use Altars and build stairs literally to the top (Lets game it out for example). It's a ton of fun creating basements, caves, and treehouses using this system as well.  7. The story - I really enjoy that there is so much lore spread out in the game. It really shows the devs put a lot of time and effort into creating a world that told a story to it. The NPC's you rescue bring so much life into the game as long as you're willing to read.   The Cons: (or in this case, needs to be worked on to improve the game)  1. The quest system. I had to rollback my cloud in order to finish a quest, "The Morning Grind", due to me accidentally pickaxing a skeletons body that I had to interact with and remove a ring from. I think making quest related interactions invincible would fix this simple bug. Also, while playing in co-op, my partner doesn't always get the quests when I interact with certain items or lore.  2. Combat - My biggest frustration is getting into a fight and not being able to lock onto the target I want to in an easier way. For example, if i use a wand or a bow, sometimes the lock will target the enemy in the back instead of the guy in my face stabbing me with his sword. Sometimes I want to shoot a barrel to take out a group but instead my wand targets the guy next to the barrel instead and then I lose that opportunity. Now, I've learned how to work with this, sword enemies up close, dodge/blink back and wand enemies at mid range while using my bow to blow up barrels with free aim but swapping between my weapons on my action bar isn't always the easiest in a fight. I think there should be an easier lock on system, not sure how, but I have hopes. Oh, and make a way to block with a bow because that would be realistic.  3. HEAL CHANNEL - Please make it so i can right click or left click in order to heal others or heal myself. It's a nice cheap spell for healing and that simple change would be huge for early/mid game mages.  4. Pets/NPC's - They LOVE to get stuck in walls or furniture! Also, is there a way to code the npcs to return to their spots when set to 0m after going to bed? I would enjoy that if so. Like they walk to their beds at night and then return back to their spots.  5. Map - I would like to see more clarity of the different zones on the map. You learn them eventually but I think this would benefit early/mid game for people who don't explore as much. That way when they need to get supplies, they know where to go easier.   Again, this game is one of the best I've ever played. I can't wait to sink in more hours as content continues to be released!

text: Want a meticulously hand-crafted world like Skyrim? Want a building system as detailed as Minecraft, or as easy as Fallout 4? Want an open world survival experience like Valheim? Want a dungeon diving experience like Assassins Creed Odyssey? Want to dig tunnels and make caves with what Geo-Mod games like Red Faction should've been?  Enshrouded has it all in one. It feels like it takes the best mechanics out of all those games, and wraps it up into one game. I've been playing 20 hours, and still only have the plains areas explored and there is so much to look at and so many places to go and see. And because its not a procedurally generated world, the details are nice to find.  All the weapons so far are fun to play with. Archery, magic, and melee combat is all pretty solid. Of the 3, range is the best, but give it time and I'm sure the hand to hand combat will be smoothed out.  So far, quirks are pretty limited, nothing game breaking so far. Setting up your own dedicated server is a piece of cake, and seems to utilize multi-core processors nicely (C'mon Microsoft, Minecraft STILL runs on 1 core for a server).  I do like how the terrain can be fully modified, from digging tunnels and blasting holes into mountains, it feels like a fully open geo-mod engine from the Red Faction games of the old days. However I noticed that after serveral days, it feels like the world does a reset, so things you did around the world, gets reset to 0. I don't know if this is by design or not, but it does make revisiting old places more interesting.  There is already easily a hundred hours of content here if you enjoy those open world survival style games or games like Skyrim. Excited to see what lies ahead.  Edit: With the Mire update, never have I seen a place that both looks as beautiful as the jungle of Sumeru from Genshin Impact, and the end result of a public restroom during free taco Tuesday at Taco Bell at the same time.  Edit 2: With the Frozen Frontier update... these devs are really flexing their creative muscle. The region is absolutely huge, diverse, and full of really cool castles to explore. And there is still tons of empty map left, which makes me even more excited to see what is around the corner in the world of Embervale!  Edit 3: Wow with the Thralls of Twilight, the atmosphere is exponentially improved, from the lighting, to the sheer amount of foliage that is in the world, making it feel more full and flush. Areas that you think you know, will feel totally different, like being unable to see the bridge from the starting meadow. I recommend playing each major update with a new character and new world (you can host your own dedicated server to do this so you can save your work).  Also discovered this game will run great on a 6gb nVidia 980ti, medium preset at 60fps.  Edit 4: Full Release! They have done a TON of work to the game in the year between major updates. If you haven't already, make a new character, start a new world, grab some friends, and get Enshrouded!  After 774 hours, I saw the credits roll. It brought a tear to my eye. Its been a hell of a journey, and its just the beginning!

text: Gonna just cut to the chase on this one,   The game itself is fantastic, the world feels amazing and full of things to do but that is also a problem, if you play on a server with more than a few of you, the world will not regen its monsters, loot, resources or anything for that matter as its on a 2 hour refresh rate that can also have that timer reset if someone enters that area, this paired with the fact quests are not shared nor the progress and can cause issues for others to not allow them to finish them is a huge flaw in the co-op aspect, and well also this game was marketed heavy towards co-op and multiplayer even the launch trailer was co-op heavy.  I saw a review stating the game seemed more catered to the single player survival game, and i cant help but shake that feeling that this game is more appealing if played as single player as opposed to playing with friends.  If your a person who plays solo in survival games then i can openly recommend this game and hope that you enjoy, However if you play survival crafting games to play with friends, explore and farm materials, I cant recommend right now as this game seems to punish you for playing with others.

text: Enshrouded is a good game with a lot of potential, but it lacks enemy variety and long-term motivation.  One of my biggest criticisms is how static the world feels. Enemies stay within their designated areas and never seem to react to the player's growing presence. You can build an impressive base, but nobody ever attacks it. The world simply doesn't care that you're there.  It would be much more exciting if enemy scouting parties actively searched for player bases. Once discovered, enemies could launch attacks that gradually increase in strength as they recognize the player as a growing threat.  This would give base building a real purpose beyond decoration and create a much more dynamic, challenging, and immersive world.  Enshrouded has a great foundation, but without more intelligent enemies, meaningful threats, and evolving challenges, the long-term gameplay becomes repetitive.

text: One of my top games of all time, up there with my beloved Skyrim! There's so much I love about this game. It's gorgeous! The foggy atmosphere of the shroud, or the beautiful views from a mountain top. The whole game has felt like a real journey. It's a handcrafted world, with loads of interesting places to explore, loot to be found and enemies to be fought! I really love how the lore is slowly uncovered via notes, and you need to revisit notes (in the journal) to really piece together the story of the world (also easy to ignore if you don't care about that!). The game is also highly customisable to play however you prefer. Not just a simple difficulty slider, you can change the combat, difficulty, resource gathering, death settings, all kind of things. And you can focus on what you care about. The base building is my favourite of any game (and I've played a lot of games like this!), but if you just want to get to the action you can easily live in pre-built structure and just do it up a bit. The game is marketed as multiplayer, but it is very playable solo as well. I have only played solo! There's probably a million things more I could say, but this is a brilliant fun survival, crafting, exploration game.

text: This game is so good, i wanna play 24/7 XD everything from visuals, music, mining, farming, crafting to combat is great - controls/UI very intuitive - the building system is PHENOMENAL !!!! you can get lost easily for hours ( or days !! ) creating your base or a whole village,  block by block XD trying different styles and layouts, there's so many materials to work with - builder heaven \o/  i just finished rebuilding a half destroyed town up north, with a friend - we stumbled upon it during a quest and fell in love with the layout of the town and buildings .. now we're spending our time fixing walls, bridges, roofs, decorating rooms instead of being out there beating up baddies XD I never played a game where the player could change already existing buildings to that extent, that's a first for me ! Having the 5 NPCs like the blacksmith, hunter, farmer etc live on your base is also a nice touch, makes it feel even more like a home :)   The wide variety of weapons, armor, spells & potions and impressive skill trees also allows for a plethora of different builds ! text: Enshrouded : A Promising Foundation Buried Under Frustration Some call it the best survival game, others the best action RPG. Few games have left me as conflicted as Enshrouded. Don't get me wrong, Enshrouded has genuine qualities. But it also carries a weight of frustrations and missed opportunities that are hard to ignore.  - Combat : Souls-Inspired But Poorly Executed The combat system clearly draws inspiration from souls-likes, but feels unfinished and archaic even after the recent combat update. Melee is at a severe disadvantage compared to ranged, not just in power, but how it feels. Every action, whether attacking or dodging, locks you into a 0.5+ second animation with no way to cancel. Getting surrounded by three enemies means getting infinitely staggered while your own attacks don't stagger them at all. The parry window is too lenient, you can parry on the very first frame and it always works, which makes it feel cheap rather than satisfying. The dodge on the other hand feels half-broken, with i-frames that seem to exist on paper only, you'll take damage mid-roll constantly. Heavy attacks hitting only a single target even when enemies are standing side by side is baffling. The camlock takes ages to reorient when an enemy moves behind you. Enemy AI is inconsistent, some won't detect you standing right in front of them, even hitting them while others get stuck in walls and fall through the floor when hit. Daggers are arguably the worst offender, weak, with a single animation, and stealth as a playstyle is essentially non-existent. Ranged combat avoids most of these issues but becomes incredibly monotonous, you'll repeat the exact same actions for dozens of hours with no variation. This was a major complaint at launch and unfortunately remains unchanged. You can't hold left click to attack continuously, which is particularly painful when playing with a wand. You also can't hold E to loot you'll be mashing your key to collect 100 plants one by one. The enemy variety is disappointing, you'll encounter the same enemies from the beginning all the way to level 35+, even if the bestiary becomes slightly more varied in later areas  - Gathering & Exploration : Tedious And Unrewarding Chopping wood is painful. You're animation-locked for the entire duration, it's not satisfying, and the inconsistency is maddening, why do I have to manually pick up wood but not ore when mining? Mining is slightly better but still lacks impact and feels unrewarding. Exploration is centered entirely around the glider, which works well enough, but the absence of mounts means you'll spend a lot of time simply running. The lack of a climbing system is a missed opportunity that would have made the world feel far more dynamic. Points of interest are hit or miss, many feel empty or pointless, and some are outright copy-pasted, including certain elixir wells that share the same layout with chests spawning in the exact same spot.  - Atmosphere & Visuals : A Genuine Highlight This is where Enshrouded genuinely shines. The world is beautiful across every biome, forests, snow, underwater. I've found myself stopping multiple times just to take in the atmosphere, especially in forested areas. The weather system is alive and dynamic, particularly in snowy regions. However, it rains almost constantly, and the endurance debuff it applies nearly every day gets old fast. Night has a fantastic atmosphere and even offers exclusive resources, but it's undermined by near-total darkness with no real solution. You can carry a torch, but you can't fight with one in hand. A belt lantern would have been an obvious and elegant fix. The Shroud is the biggest visual offender. Visibility is already poor, but pulling out a torch in there effectively flashbangs you. The blue visual effects add to the blindness more than the atmosphere. The art direction overall is excellent, environments, enemies, armor sets, weapons and cosmetics all look astonishing.  - Crafting & Base Building : Deep But Overwhelming Enshrouded arguably has the best base building in its genre in terms of sheer possibility, a massive variety of materials, pieces and customisation options. I do miss the structural integrity system from Valheim, but that's a personal preference. That said, the depth comes at a cost. The number of different workshops is overwhelming, and it's genuinely confusing to remember which one does what. Workshops don't pull from nearby chests, which means constant manual inventory management. Upgrading a chest requires emptying it, removing it, and replacing it, a baffling design choice. The sheer number of different resources compounds this, you'll regularly feel lost in your own inventory. Crafting from your inventory, from NPCs and from various workshops simultaneously creates redundancy without clarity. The building process itself is clunky, you craft pieces at a workbench, then switch to your hammer, scroll through options and select the right material. It works but it's a headache.  - Quests & Progression : Fedex With Style The NPC quest system is extensive, which is genuinely useful for players who don't enjoy pure sandbox gameplay, it gives you a clear direction to follow. But it quickly becomes repetitive and Ubisoft-like in its structure. The gameplay loop overall lacks depth and variety. It's enjoyable at first but fades into repetition sooner than it should. On the positive side, the talent tree is varied and readable, and the ability to reset your stats easely to experiment with different builds is a great quality of life feature. Loot is decent, legendaries appear regularly without completely invalidating other rarities, which keeps things balanced.  - Hollow Halls : The Best Part Of The Game The dungeons called Hollow Halls are genuinely impressive. Large, dense with enemies and full of atmosphere. Walking into my first skeleton invasion, I felt like I was in the scene from Lord of the Rings where Aragorn, Legolas and Gimli face the Army of the Dead. That's a compliment. The level 35 Hollow Hall though... let's just say it's a bit of a middle finger and leave it at that.  Final thoughts Enshrouded has real strengths, stunning visuals, excellent art direction, deep base building, solid RPG systems and a massive amount of content. But it's weighed down by combat that lacks depth and polish, overwhelming crafting systems, tedious gathering, and a gameplay loop that runs out of steam too quickly. The game is noticeably more enjoyable in co-op, which helps paper over some of its weaknesses. There's a genuinely great game somewhere in here. It's just not fully there yet.

text: You can feel how much passion and love went into this game. The world is very stunningly large and detailed, the graphics are beautiful and there's a lot of stuff to do to keep you occupied for many hours.  But the main game loop is shallow and grindy.  The main thing to do in the game is to chase question marks on your map, killing enemies on the way, sometimes search for a quest item (or button/lever), return to your base, spend 20 minutes organizing your inventory and chests, grind to get geared up again and repeat. The "killing enemies" bit is fun at times, but gets stale rather quick, because there isn't much enemy variety. The same enemy types get recycled over and over again, but only with higher "level numbers". After 25 hours in, I'm still facing the same boars from the beginning of the game, and they're still as deadly as they've been in the beginning, because in the new areas they have the level number "19" instead of "3" over their heads.  Abilities in the game are tied to items, which you need to equip in order to use them. You can't just start building - you need to equip the building hammer first before you can enter build mode (which takes up a valuable inventory slot). You can't just cast a fire spell with the press of the button. You need to actively equip a staff, hold right mouse button use your scroll wheel to select it and then charge it with the left mouse button. It's tedious.  Then there is the grind. Crafting requires a lot of different resources and relatively large quantities of them. You'll constantly need to set out and gather basic materials in order to progress or even just craft ammunition. Even building blocks require a lot of resources. And there's something I have never seen in a game before: Wizards spells require not only mana but [b]ammunition[/b]. And I'm not talking about "scrolls" for unique, powerful spells. Your basic spells like Fireball and Ice Bolt require ammo to be cast. And how do you get a reliable amount of ammo? By grinding and crafting.  Yes, you do get unlimited variants of the spells over time, but 25 hours in I only have the Ice Bolt spell. text: so an overview of what it is like relative to other survival games (its not particularly survival):  No rotting/expiration of food you don't drop Tools on death, just materials no carry weight, just slots building system is extremely generous, you get a lot of pieces for pretty low initial resources no hunger/thirst, just valheim type benefits for foods (game is basically valheim, in many ways, and then changed in others) can fast travel between Flame Altars, their equivalent of the workbench in valheim or the C.A.M.P from fallout, its the building zone and you start being able to have two, and that is upgradeable terrain/resources respawn outside of player claimed zones character creator is extremely simple, very much like valheim's so not a lot there (although for whatever reason they literally have a bunch of BG3 hairs, i don't think its like ripped models, its just the same hairstyles lol) a single world, not procedurally generated, it is like Ark in that it is a story map, so there are old structures from the kingdom that used to be there their roads and paths in this kingdom reduce the amount of stamina consumed by sprinting, so you are encouraged to use their roads. text: Enshrouded is one of the best games I'm ever going to [i]not[/i] recommend.  Let's start with the good, because there is a lot of it!  This game features a ridiculously huge world, massive biomes, sprawling dungeons and a long list of things to do. If you're looking to burn time you can't go far wrong.  Probably the most impressive thing to me is the technical proficiency. The rendering and presentation is phenomenal! Beautiful landscapes, astounding lighting, and a good variety of assets. For nearly 150 hours I played this game and continued to have "Oh wow that looks amazing" moments right through to the end. Often it was while looking at many of the same assets as I had already seen, but the lights, rays, tints and shadows had cast them in delightful new arrangements.  And the technical proficiency extends to the building mechanics, the landscape terraforming, the water physics, the farming and the crafting. Building a house (or base complex) and collecting villagers to live there has been stellar. Properly digging in the grounds of a sand dune or ruined temple complex to reveal a buried body, chest, or crypt entrance - not faked but actually doing it - were standout moments! The quality and level of detail has lain an incredible foundation. Real talent. I think Enshrouded could easily be one of the best games of all time with these fundamentals. I'm serious.  But unfortunately there are significant aspects of the game that remain too barebones or underdeveloped.  [list] [*]First, the combat is very primitive and seriously held back by dodgy targeting and frustrating footwork that can often see your character lunging in odd directions. I probably died more to lethal falls than anything else - and the longer I played the more frustrating that experience became.  [*]Enemy variety is extremely low, and there is an absence of meaningful large set pieces. Yes you occasionally find a large monster but they are quickly recycled and lose their magic. The one genuinely unique and fancy set-piece is a [spoiler]dragon battle[/spoiler] which is probably one of the most badly tuned and miserable combat encounters I've played in the past five years. Yes, there is a lot to do here but it all feels the same: Run around and press F while hacking apart hordes of the same enemies. In almost every dungeon and shroud excursion the same thought would always come to me before the end: [i]This is taking far too long.[/i]  [*]The story might well be interesting but I wouldn't know. It is delivered in a terribly thin and unappetizing manor. Hunting for unvoiced skippable walls of text around the environment turns out to just not be interesting enough. I am not the kind of player who places a particularly high value on voice acting but Enshrouded would seriously benefit from more of it, as well as infrequent cutscenes to punctuate major storyline moments or access to new biomes.  [*]There is too much shroud! (Either that, or the experiences in the shroud need to be more diverse.) I know that may seem like a foolish thing to critique given the name of the game, but the truth is that the shroud is a dreary, bland, washed out place that just isn't fit for being the place we spend the majority of our game time. All those generous compliments I just paid to the games rendering above? Well don't get too attached to them because you will spend most of your time walking through a grey mist. [/list]  The word I can best use to sum up Enshrouded is "Ambitious". And that's a statement that cuts both ways. This game has a great baseline but what it needs now is content to fill it. Unfortunately [i]Keen Games[/i] development focus seems to be stacking new biomes on to the end of the progression and I feel this is a mistake. There is a reason that only 1% of players on steam have killed the dragon: It's because everything leading up to that is currently too sprawling and too boring. Who really cares if you add another biome after it?  I think Enshrouded needs the equivalent of maybe 3 major DLC's, each with significant content injections for prior areas, before I can recommend it. But don't give up [i]Keen Games[/i], you have something remarkable if you play your cards right.

text: Not quite there, but could be great someday  Enshrouded is a survival adventure rpg that encourages you to gather a group of friends and explore a fallen world covered in a deadly mythical mist. Despite this concept, I don't think any component of the game is great and it fails to balance each element of gameplay in a manner that I find fun or interesting.  Starting with survival, it is a rather simple system needlessly complicated by strange mechanics that just complicates things. It is not really a survival game, rather the survival elements are just a means of progression. You can't starve or die of thirst or anything like that. Food, water, and potions are all solely for buffs. You have the ability to base build and you can even find npcs to join your base. The problem with this is that your progression to greater tech and items are locked behind these npcs which you will have to talk to each and every time you want to craft something. Want specific armor, you have to craft it through the right npc. want potions, only an npc can help you craft it. want to make something more complicated than charred meat on a stick? well you need an npc for that. They also have unique crafting stations, and these have the annoying element of requiring time in order to make them, leading to the whole experience being sluggish and overly complicated. This isn't even talking about gathering the material, which there is too much of and yet never enough for a full party without a lot of grind. In general, I think this system needs an overhaul like having your crafting bench have items based off of who is at your base so that all your crafting options are on one menu. I would also increase certain resources or make a map that better marks where to find them. Otherwise you have a whole lot of ground to cover in order to find the one thing needed for progression.  In terms of an Adventure RPG it fairs a bit better. The game includes dungeons, bosses, and many unique areas to wander and discover things in. Part of the reason I think crafting certain items takes so long is to have something waiting for you after a day of adventuring. It is required for you to explore to progress the game and your base. For the most part you will get your weapons from adventuring too. My biggest problems with adventuring is that it can be very unrewarding at times, and that the class system isn't very fun. There are a lot of different weapons you can use in this game, and if you play with friends you will probably diversify what type of weapons you are using. Unfortunately, finding a weapon for yourself can be very grindy and you might make several stops at different places on the map without much to show for it. You also don't normally find armor while adventuring and need to craft it, so it can be a huge slog to start a new area with higher level enemies who eat your hits like its nothing but deal out a lot of damage every attack. Some classes have an easier time with this but there are also just bad options too. I played an archer most of my playthrough with friends and it was very frustrating to deal with the high resource cost along with mediocre damage. Then I switched to two handed warrior and I was dealing 3 times as much damage while also having natural regen and defense to spare. I heard the devs have been balancing a lot of classes and I suspect archers are a victim of this. I would recommend balancing classes to make them fun rather than to make them fair. I will say, the dungeons in the game are still very fun and play out almost like a raid in an MMO. When the game is more structured and linear in a dungeon it feels a lot better to play and interact with. Even as a boring class like archer, I still wanted to go out there and explore.  I don't hate this game, but it is flawed and still needs a lot more time. I had some issues with graphics and visuals that were annoying too, but those are things I figure will be patched out eventually. I'd love to see where this game sits in a few years after a few big updates, and I hope some of my issues with gameplay get resolved then. I'd still say get it on sale if its cheap enough, It can be fun with a group, epsecially at later levels when you have your build going.

text: I really love Enshrouded, but the frequent performance and stability issues are making it almost unplayable right now.  The game regularly crashes due to what appears to be a GPU-related error, which often results in the game (or even Steam/PC) dumping and closing. Crash frequency is inconsistent — sometimes I can play for an hour, other times it happens after just 15 minutes. Each crash means lost progress, which is incredibly frustrating.  I have a high-end rig and Enshrouded is the only game I experience these issues with, so it doesn’t seem to be a specs problem. I’ve already sunk over 50 hours into it and genuinely enjoy the game when it’s running smoothly, but the instability has reached the point where I’m hesitant to even launch it.  This seems to be a fairly common issue based on the forums. I really hope the devs address it soon — the game has so much potential but it's hard to recommend in its current state.

text: Enshrouded is what you’d get if Minecraft, Valheim, and Elden Ring had a very ambitious child who never quite learned optimisation. You start off naked, smacking trees, thinking this is just another survival-crafting game. Then suddenly, a ghost fog appears and you’re getting steamrolled by a monster wearing your grandmother’s curtains.  Building feels great, it's snappy and intuitive. Combat? Surprisingly deep, especially when you realise dodging actually matters and magic doesn’t just exist to look pretty. But then the Shroud hits, and everything becomes a Soulslike horror film where stamina is a cruel joke and light sources are more precious than your actual friends.  It’s got co-op, base building, RPG elements, and just enough jank to keep things interesting. Basically, it's a chaotic buffet of genres where every dish tries to kill you. Highly recommended if your friend group enjoys dying together while arguing over who forgot to light the torches.

text: Overall, a 6/10 game, mainly because one of the core pillars is depressingly badly implemented at the moment. - almost everything is executed perfectly, from base building, to farming, to exploration, to collectables, to gorgeous and plentiful armor sets, but combat feels absolutely terrible...  There are hundreds of quests, each with a story, that all add to an exceptionally well done world building full of lore and intrigue and drama in an age long past. A bit sad and gloomy, but enjoyable and a treat to go through and read about.  The base feels lively and comfy due to both the amazing building & decoration capabilities and the NPCs you can rescue and... er... adopt(?) I guess, that roam around you base if you let them.  Where it still needs improvement is the combat, which, imo, is the weakest part of the game. While melee is at least passable, with the caveat that dodges have no iframes (really, really bad choice), and blocking/parries are jank as hell and the timings are atrocious, and finally that melee itself has no inherent "combo" moves at all (you can spec into a couple, but no heavy/light attack or after-parry repostes for example).  Magic is absolute garbage. Literal trash on fire. The staff is NOT a combat weapon, it is a "stand as far back as possible and lob spells until all is dead" tool of disjointed, boring destruction. You cannot parry or block with the staff, and you cannot bonk with the staff. Wands are somehow worse. The staff at least has SOME oompf (fireballs go boom), but the wands are like pissing on the enemy and somehow they die. No stagger on hit, annoying auto-lock-on that I wish was toggle-able, and, cherry on cake, neither wands nor staves can do any sort of finisher or combo moves.  Honestly magic feels like you become this glorified turret. Your only button is Left Click. No combos with jumps or dodges or whatever, just left click at enemy and watch hp bar go down.  Combat needs a total rework - keep the talents like jump-smash and the dodge-attack, but give all weapons a lot more moves, and magic, especially, a lot more flexibility and just stuff to do with.  Now, some might say "but a 6/10 should be recommended!" - to this I say "No, not yet. When they rework combat, add more enemy variety, and make blocking, dodging, and magic not suck phalluses, then I'll change it to positive and give the game a 9/10".  I eagerly await a ton of bug-fixes, performance improvements and a combat rework, these Devs appear to be competent and listening, so I'm cautiously hopeful.  Edit: I want to be more fair as to just how bad combat is:  Enemies, even the weakest ones, always stagger you on hit. 2+ enemies can effectively stunlock you... however YOU cannot stunlock THEM. In fact, no weapon, regardless of size or speed, staggers enemies AT ALL. This completely breaks the flow of combat, since you have to spam block/parry mid-attack since the enemy doesn't care it was just whacked with a huge 2h hammer in the face. You have no poise, yet enemies have infinite poise. How is this fair?  Melee builds (1h + shield, 2h) have no adequate answer for big flying enemies. Small flying enemies can be "pulled" to you and you can quickly whack them, but big ones = death trap. You will pull yourself to them and promptly miss any attack and fall to your death or be forced to glide down. The only actual answer is a bow... which is not buffed by any melee-based stat (Strength). So you just stand there, dodging annoying homing projectiles, while you unload 10 arrows into some flying blob.  Magic also has no adequate answer for big flying enemies, since wands don't have the range, and staves have ammo + no homing + mana cost + slow cast = a long, long time to kill.  Edit: Ranged (Bow) and Daggers. That is all. Finally good gameplay, shame all the other weapons are either bad or simply mediocre.  Edit: Disabling comments as I don't want to deal with "Haha made a typo, your review is bad lolololol". Grow up.

text: A builders/crafters dream.  This game as is, even in early access, is one of the best voxel based builders I've experienced.  Collecting resources isn't tedious and the ability to craft a ton of building materials means the game encourages you to build BIG.  If you ever felt like creating your own castle or city or underground Dwarven fortress this is the game to get. That being said the RPG elements are nice and compliment the game play but still need some refinement but if you just want a chill game where you can escape and literally terraform your own hobbit home out of any random set of hills, this is for you. It takes elements from many popular games out there and utilizes them very well, and from a developer that doesn't have a history of big games I'm loving this one, can't wait for future updates and what the full release will look like.
