text: This is one of those games that.... while you technically *can* play it solo, you really ought to think of it as a pure multiplayer game.  Everything about this game is tuned, designed, and optimized to be enjoyed by a group of people.  I played through the solo experience so far for a good 13 hours or so and... I mean it works, but it really doesn't have the depth of most single player games.  It's a bit of an open world slop builder that expects you to be part of a group of people gathering resources or heading out to do something together.  The building system here is pretty good.... it's not the best I've played, but its good.  It definitely has a huge variety of pieces, so you can make almost anything... but alignment and leveling and world grid options seem to be something that weren't really thought through and can lead to some frustrating situations with your builds.  Especially if you are trying to connect two structures.  The land leveling works ok, but its very labor intensive.  The combat is fun.  I actually enjoy the combat for the most part.... but some of the bosses just aren't fair in first person.  They are clearly meant to have you spread out and have someone distracting the boss while others are attacking from the flanks or rear, or sending in magic or arrows.... but as a solo player you are pretty much limited to dodging around a lot.  I like the game, I really do.  I just don't think it's a good solo game, and if you are looking for a good, immersive solo combat/crafting/base building experience, this isn't it.  If you have a group of friends though, well you would be hard pressed to find anything better.

text: I haven't been genuinely excited about a new game since Baldur's Gate 3 and Valheim, but this one completely caught me off guard.  I'm about 72 hours in and still haven't upgraded my Fire Altar to level 2. Not because I can't, but because I simply haven't needed to. There's so much to explore, build, experiment with, and discover on other players' maps that I've barely scratched the surface.  As someone who has played a ton of RPG, survival, and building games, the building system was one of the biggest surprises. It's intuitive, flexible, and honestly one of the best I've used.  What stood out for me:  I picked it up for $40, and it feels like it's worth far more than that. Grinding is kept to a minimum, while resources are abundant and varied. Building is incredibly smooth and satisfying, especially after the latest update. I love Valheim's building system, but this feels even more polished and user-friendly. The lore book update is fantastic. I usually don't stop to read every page of lore in games, but having it narrated while you continue exploring feels like listening to a well-acted audiobook. On top of that, the lore often contains useful information that helps uncover secrets, puzzles, and hidden items. The graphics are gorgeous, and I can actually run the game on high settings without issues. Combat and movement feel responsive and satisfying so far.  Honestly, other developers should take notes. This game has come an incredibly long way.  The crazy part is that I still feel like I've experienced less than 10% of what the game has to offer. Even so, the 1.0 update has already pushed it into the category of the best games I've played in years.  One thing I always do in RPG, survival, and building games is find creative ways to use the tools the developers give me to make the experience more immersive. This game skips that step and puts those tools directly in the player's hands from the start. It genuinely feels like the game wants you to create, experiment, and play your own way.  Highly recommended.

text: I really want to like this game but they make it so difficult for me to.  Dear god the amount of fucking crafting stations in this game is unbelievable. I found that I needed to expand my base quite a few times, not because I needed more storage, not because I wanted to have more decoration or anything, but PURELY just because of the sheer number of crafting stations. There are about 27 crafting stations in the game (at the time I'm writing this), and most of them look like they would all do the same thing. I don't get why there needs to be 5 different types of furnaces when we could have just 1 to smelt ores into ingots. If anything I would've hoped that they would be upgradable, but they just aren't. My base might as well just be a factory without automation at this point. On top of that you also need to house multiple NPCs in your base, some of which are also used to craft items, and others that at least have shops.  The combat isn't good at all either. Every attack I do just locks me in a super long animation that I cant break out of. If I attack at the slightly wrong time then I just get shredded by enemies. The dodge mechanics in combat are absolutely horrible. Whenever you dodge you just collide with an enemy and get stopped. The skill tree in game looked promising but half the skills I used were so insignificant or hardly noticeable that I didn't feel like they helped at all. I can't lie though, the major bosses in the game are pretty fun to fight, unique looking bosses and fight mechanics, but unfortunately some of the less major bosses tend to be re used in quite a few places.  The most positive thing I can say about this game, is that the world exploration is pretty fun. You can craft a glider and soar around areas, different biomes to explore that are fairly unique from one another.  The base building is definitely better than what I've seen in some other games. Enshrouded uses a type of voxel system, meaning bases are made out of smaller cubes that make up walls and floors. With this you can get some more creative structures and designs for your home.

text: With the official release scheduled for this autumn, as a "beginner" with over 1,700 hours, I must warn you about the recent state of the game.  Note: 1,500 of my hours were spent BEFORE the recent garbage updates. The remaining 200 hours were spent purely testing and verifying bugs for reports.  The Good:  Respec items are cheap, making build experimentation accessible.  Walking while swinging a pickaxe is convenient.  Armor pieces now grant skill nodes (though you still have to manually unlock them with points, unlike Monster Hunter). Pure elemental mage is fun.  Dodge rolls now have actual invincibility frames (iframes).  The Bad (Bugs & Unpolished Mechanics):  Artificial Level Caps: Gear can be upgraded to Lv54, but it is programmed to force-reset back to Lv50 upon relogging. All grinding effort is completely wasted.  Ruined Glider Physics: Closing the glider immediately after using "Updraft" completely kills your upward momentum (it carried over naturally before). Switching weapons while gliding locks you out of the skill entirely.  Flawed Heavy Attacks: There are no "Super Armor" frames during the startup animation. Getting hit instantly cancels it (especially noticeable on Two-Handed Swords). If it clips into static objects, hitboxes fail to register on enemies.  Downgrades & Systemic Failures:  Text Restrictions: You can no longer use line breaks on signs or in the chat bar.  The Pickaxe Nerf: You can no longer use the pickaxe or axe while jumping. The devs hated players reaching high places too easily, but you can still just dig diagonally while walking. Jumping to dig was High-Risk, High-Reward (stamina drain, steep cliffs). Digging while walking is safe and brainless (Low-Risk, High-Reward). What was the point of this change?  Clunky Woodcutting: A slow wind-up animation was added to the first swing of the axe. Now you get constantly staggered by stray trash mobs before the first hit connects unless you wipe out the entire area first.  Skill Tree Bloat & Role Destruction: They split existing skills into tiers and filled the tree with generic HP nodes, ruining class identity. They increased the required points just to reach pre-update performance. Tanks lost their passive aggro multiplier and got a clunky active percentage buff instead. Healers now pull massive aggro that tanks can't out-damage. Backline squishies (bow/magic) are constantly targeted and deleted.  Psychic AI & Broken Rendering: Enemies perfectly dodge projectiles fired from stealth at extreme distances. Flying enemies dodge mid-air as if kicking off solid ground. Furthermore, objects and enemies frequently fail to render at all, even on "Performance" settings. It feels heavily like they cannot maintain their own codebase.  Response to the Developers / Community Management: Recently, a user was spamming toxic rants ("this game is trash") on the forums. To keep the community healthy, I posted constructive solutions, layout strategies adjusting to the flawed AI pathfinding, and creative gameplay workarounds.  In response, my posts were deleted and I was permanently BAN-ned from the community hub by the moderators.  According to the development team's moderation logic:  To give you an idea of what they censor vs. what they tolerate:  ALLOWED: Toxic posts by a player spending 2.5 hours on a starter dungeon that normally takes only 1 hour solo, only to rant that the rewards are "garbage"—even though modest rewards are perfectly appropriate for an early-game dungeon, and the delay was 100% a skill issue.  ALLOWED: Build discussions that openly assume utilizing past exploits to get 188 skill points instead of the intended 184 cap.  DELETED/CENSORED: Creative strategy guides suggesting players fly over the center of a 3D maze instead of walking through it.  DELETED/CENSORED: Common-sense layout advice suggesting players design their bases around the flawed pathfinding of the game's AI.  The developers run their own community management. By banning constructive advice while tolerating toxicity, it’s clear they don’t care about player feedback ahead of the 1.0 launch.  Conclusion: They are no longer fixing this game. Blatantly obvious bugs that anyone would catch in a single test play are popping up daily. It’s highly probable they have no QA environment left, and are just drip-feeding hard-locked content to meet their autumn release deadline.  Relying on Early Access as an excuse to stretch playtime by killing player convenience and leaving critical code unmaintained is a toxic trend. text_full: With the official release scheduled for this autumn, as a "beginner" with over 1,700 hours, I must warn you about the recent state of the game. The Good:  Respec items are cheap, making build experimentation accessible.  Walking while swinging a pickaxe is convenient.  Armor pieces now grant skill nodes (though you still have to manually unlock them with points, unlike Monster Hunter). Pure elemental mage is fun.  Dodge rolls now have actual invincibility frames (iframes).  The Bad (Bugs & Unpolished Mechanics):  Artificial Level Caps: Gear can be upgraded to Lv54, but it is programmed to force-reset back to Lv50 upon relogging. All grinding effort is completely wasted.  Ruined Glider Physics: Closing the glider immediately after using "Updraft" completely kills your upward momentum (it carried over naturally before). text: This game is amazing. Basically Valheim but IMO better than valheim was when it first released and honestly can hold its own against present valheim. Mostly all positives but there are a couple things i would like to see changed. For one, setting options like palworlds has would be nice, being able to switch loot dropping on death to it not dropping on death. I honestly hate that in survival games considering its not a difficulty thing per say, its just a time consuming thing which imo is a waste of time. I wanna be exploring and doing productive things not going back to my dead body cuz i accidentally slipped off a ledge into fire. Again imo thats not difficulty its literally just wasting the gamers time. I also came across a little issue with roots, playing coop in my cousins hosted game, i destroyed a root when he wasnt there and he didnt get the skill point for it and when he went to the spot the root was still gone. we thought he might be screwed out of the point but we just had to restart the server. but what if your playing on a server you pay for thats always online, then what? Another little nit pick, the hit boxes sometimes seem a little wonky, example ill be standing completely behind an enemy and theyll swing, the axe makes no contact with me yet i take damage..  Again tho those are little nit picks cuz overall without question i recommend buying this game. Shit I wouldve paid 59.99 for this game, its far better than some triple A titles! I love the variety in skill tree, might of put double jump inside the circle  with skills like the wood cutting and mining skills, rather than on one of the class part of the tree but again this is an opinion based nit pick. The building in the game is SOOO good. The fact you can place square by square for roof and wall pieces, most games just have full walls and limited roof pieces.. Im excited to see 6 months from now some of the insane builds people come up with.  THE MAP IS INSANELY LARGE.. i was shocked at how big this map is. I would say this game is basically Valheim had a baby with Breath of the wild with a dash of minecraft. if you enjoy any of those games, BUY THIS GAME

text: I've really enjoyed playing this game so far H O W E V E R, Even though I haven't finished it yet, I'm finding the last section of the game (levels 18-25) reaaaally tedious and boring. Having played both Valheim and Dying Light 2 I recognize a lot of the mechanics (the shroud is basically the dark zones in DL2 and A LOT of skills in the skill tree are the same as well, glider, glider updraft, shooting bow in slo-mo while mid-air, etc.  Pros: - building is nice - different career paths (ranged, melee, mage) - the farming isn't obnoxious Cons: - You can't pause the game when you're playing alone. WHY? Most co-op games allow you to pause as long as you're playing by yourself. And this is especially necessary if you have to pause while being in the shroud (in which you slowly die). - Stealth SUCKS, it's almost impossible to make stealth kills because enemies never stand still, they are always patrolling one next to another covering their blind spots and their detection skills are lvl 10000, plus there's always a f***ing dog, wolf, or vukah next to them and they get alerted, so all the stealth skills go to the shroud bin. - The verticality of the map: the amount of time I've wasted because "objective below" or "objective "above" in unclimbable  zones is insane. and the glider only helps if you're going down. 75% of the map are ROUND mountains, so good luck climbing. They should let you use the grappling hook more often. - The glider: While the gliding itself feels pretty good, the cancelling mechanics and sync with the double jump led to my demise more times than I want to admit. Mostly because sometimes you want to double jump down to negate fall damage but if the jump is too high the glider activates instead of letting you double jump. - The loot: I've been using the same weapons and gear for the last 15 hours of the game at least, they lack variety, don't scale very well and the farming is pretty weird, sometimes you get an amazing item for looting a random chest or side quest but then defeat a very powerful enemy and the rewards are trash. Besides, the loot level scaling locking to a specific zone is SO bad. All I do now is find legendary swords and daggers at level 12 while I'm level 24. -Skills: Some of the skills fall short and don't feel like they impact a lot in the game. For instance, in Dying Light 2, you unlock different combat moves, parkour options, etc. that make you a killing machine towards the end of the game. Here, half of the skills are character skills (damage, health, mana) and the ones that aren't feel useless. I'm technically reaching endgame and I still struggle with a lot of enemies and feel the same combat experience as when I was level 5.  Conclusion: for an early access game it's still quite enjoyable but it hasn't made me want to play it for hours on end. Sometimes I play for like 15 minutes and get bored and quit. It has a lot of potential but most of the aforementioned aspects are what make me (and some other people I've read) lose interest in the game.

text: After completing all the quests I think Enshrouded is a good game especially for being early access, it has a lot of potential to be even better.   Some things I would improve upon:  1.) It gets way too dark at night, things need to be a little more visible rather than being pitch black, or at the very least they should provide a night vision potion or night vision ability in the skill tree.  2.) The questing system needs to improve, in multiplayer especially sometimes quests get completed but it's not shared so I miss out on the XP and I have to do the mission solo. Also some quests need a checklist or a little more guidance in the description. I understand they want people to explore and find things on their own as they play but sometimes its a little too vague and confusing. They don't need to completely hold my hand, some puzzle solving and encouraging exploration is nice but there are a couple missions that seem to require a guide. For example, I never would have found all the fossils or the Blackmire crafting recipes if I didn't look it up.  3.) The map needs improvement, an elevation indicator for quest locations, flame shrines and other markers on the map and more detail would definitely help.  4.) Placing and moving furniture can be frustrating, trying to maneuver the camera in order to see the "E" indicator so you can pick up an item is frustrating especially if it's in an awkward position or if you end up picking up the wrong item. Furniture placement should be more like it is with placing building blocks.  5.) There needs to be a size indicator while crafting items so you can tell how big an item is before you craft it. Sometimes items look like they will be small but they end up a lot larger than expected.  6.) Flame shrines and sanctums should have a checkmark when you discover them so you can tell which ones you've been to and which ones you still need to find in order to make the associated achievements more fun to get.  7.) I do experience the occasional crash and graphical glitch, also it can lag for me. It might be due to an outdated graphics card so keep that in mind.  Here are things I like about the game:  1.) Building bases is awesome, the controls take a little getting used to but it's relatively easy to make something really cool and they provide a lot of variety for aesthetics. It feels pretty free. If you decide you don't like a way a wall looks it's easy to replace it with a different block. Having an undo button is really convenient as well. The base building is one of the best aspects of the game.  2.) Combat is fun, lots of skills and abilities to choose from and a good sense of progression throughout the course of playing the game. I wish there was more variety of enemies, maybe more unique enemies for each biome.  3.) Dying isn't as punishing as it is in other games, also they did a great job in making it possible to recover your items in most places you die.  4.) I like the number of different weapons and armor options in the game and the ability to enhance weapons. Some armor sets look pretty cool, and it's fun to collect items and it's easy to recycle weapons if you don't want them anymore. I wish I could recycle and upgrade armor, rings, and shields as well but maybe they'll add that later.  5.) There's a lot of variety in furnishings and decorations. I wish the bard had more banner options or if you had the ability to dye items for different aesthetics.  6.) I was really pleased with the mountain biome that came out recently, although it can be tough to navigate sometimes I think it was really well done for the most part. Also the added features like pets and farm animals as well as additional NPCs was really nice. I kind of wish you could control exactly where the NPCs go when they wander around rather than just a radius, like setting a path or restricting them to a room because they can be a little hard to find at times when they wander off.  7.) The game is really fun to play multi-player, aside from some issues with quests and the occasional lag I've been having a lot of fun playing with friends.  In conclusion, I know it sounds like I've been making a lot of complaints but overall I have enjoyed playing the game. All of the issues I have mentioned can be addressed in future updates so I look forward to the next one and looking at the roadmap it seems they are heading in the right direction. The game is already fun at this relatively early stage of development. Even after I'm done with all the missions so far I still want to play.

text: Enshrouded is a game that took me by surprise in the best of ways. It took me a while to finally decide to play this, but it was so worth it. The game itself already has a lot of content, with the developers adding more frequently.   [b] Combat: [/b] Combat in Enshrouded isn't necessarily easy, but, mechanically, it's pretty simple. You can choose between a variety of styles that pretty much cover all of the classic RPG bases. You can mix magic, stealth, and strength to fine-tune your build to match your preferred experience. High level areas do punish you pretty hard for wandering into them unprepared, but you are also awarded the same strength against lower level areas. Enemies are also varied enough. There isn't a HUGE selection of enemies, but there's enough that it doesn't feel stale.  [b] Exploring/Questing: [/b] This game has a lot of quests (maybe too many for specific things), and this truly lets you explore a good portion of the world without any extra exploring. The level differences between areas are just steep enough to keep you in one area long enough to get some questing and experience there before moving onto the next. The map itself is pretty large and takes a good amount of time to cross. The biomes are varied and fun, giving players a lot to see in each place.   [b] Building: [/b] The buildcraft part of this game is by far one of my favorites. I absolutely love the building system and the freedom it allows for. It's certainly not without its learning curve (like most base-building games), but I don't think it's anywhere close to the most difficult. The addition of NPCs that need homes is lovely because it gives a great reason to build actual settlements. The player is allowed to build multiple bases after a point, so they can all be in different places with different goals, if you so desire. The building zone for bases is also larger than I anticipated (at the highest level of flame altar). It's more than big enough for my village twice over.   Honestly, this game is easily worth the money. Enshrouded is, in my opinion, one of the best survival buildcraft games on the market right now.

text: # Enshrouded Review  I honestly think Enshrouded is becoming one of my all-time favorite games.  What surprised me most is that this game doesn’t just do one thing well. Most survival games usually have one standout feature while the rest feel shallow or unfinished. Enshrouded somehow brings combat, exploration, traversal, progression, atmosphere, and building together in a way that actually feels polished.  And somehow it’s only $30.  As I’ve gotten older, it’s become harder for games to really pull me in. A lot of games today feel repetitive or like giant checklist simulators. This game completely sucked me in. I constantly had “wow” moments while exploring.  ## Combat  The combat is honestly the best I’ve played in a survival game and competes with some AAA RPGs.  Different weapons completely change how the game feels: - sword and shield - two-handed weapons - bows - magic - movement abilities - dodge rolling - blink abilities - weapon upgrades and special effects  Combat is smooth, responsive, and actually FUN instead of just “good enough for a survival game.” Boss fights encourage exploration and upgrading rather than frustrating grind walls.  ## Exploration  The exploration is incredible. The world feels handcrafted instead of randomly generated. Every ruin, tunnel, cave, dungeon, mountain, or hidden structure feels intentionally placed.  You constantly get sidetracked in the best way possible.  You’ll head out looking for one material and suddenly spend another hour discovering: - hidden caves - giant dungeons - amazing viewpoints - waterfalls - hidden structures - new biomes  The biomes are also fantastic. Some areas genuinely made me want to move my entire base because they looked so good.  The world has that rare “wow factor.”  ## Traversal  Traversal is a huge part of why exploration feels so good.  Double jump, gliding, terrain destruction, stamina progression, and vertical world design all work together perfectly. As you level up and improve your gear, traversal becomes smoother and more enjoyable.  The game is VERY vertical and exploration actually feels like an adventure instead of simply running across flat terrain.  ## Building  This might honestly be the best building system I’ve ever used in a survival game.  The voxel-based building lets you create almost anything: - castles - underground bases - mountain homes - towns - hidden caves - bridges - giant structures  And unlike many survival games, it works for BOTH hardcore builders and casual players.  If you want to spend hundreds of hours creating insane builds, you can.  If you just want to quickly make a useful base and get back to adventuring, it works for that too.  That balance is incredibly hard to get right and this game nails it.  ## Progression  The progression pacing is excellent.  Whether you’re: - upgrading gear - unlocking skills - rescuing NPCs - finding materials - unlocking crafting stations - improving traversal - or expanding your base  …it always feels rewarding.  The game never really felt grindy to me. Even side content usually rewards you with something meaningful.  ## Criticism  The game isn’t perfect.  Farming is probably the weakest system right now. I enjoy farming in games, but Enshrouded doesn’t explain or introduce it very well compared to the rest of the mechanics.  The story is also lighter than some RPGs. There’s lore and worldbuilding, but if you’re expecting something heavily cinematic like Red Dead Redemption 2, this isn’t that type of game. Personally, I think the gameplay-first focus was the correct decision.  ## Developers / Early Access  The developers deserve serious credit.  Update 8 massively improved: - combat - progression - enemy behavior - quest flow - inventory management - quality-of-life systems  The inventory sorting system alone is amazing. You can stand on a pad in your base and automatically sort materials into nearby chests. Small features like that make a huge difference in survival games.  This genuinely feels like a dev team that listens to feedback.  Honestly, this game is so polished already that you sometimes forget it’s still Early Access.  ## Things I’d Love to See Added  - Mounts or better climbing mechanics - More decorations and building materials - More useful villagers/NPC routines - Interactive furniture - Ambient music/sound systems for bases - Hidden doors, switches, automation - Better pet behavior - Faster late-game excavation tools - More biome/world expansions - Better building material unlock systems - Base-sharing between worlds  ## Final Thoughts  After 150+ hours, I still haven’t seen everything.  There are still areas I haven’t fully explored, buildings I haven’t discovered, and bases I still want to create.  If you love: - survival games - exploration - action RPG combat - creative building - handcrafted worlds - progression systems  …this game absolutely deserves your attention.  Enshrouded doesn’t feel like “just another survival game.”  It feels like one of the few modern games that truly understands adventure, curiosity, exploration, creativity, and player freedom all at the same time.  And the craziest part is…  It’s only getting better.

text: Please note that this is a review after only 10 hours play time, after playing for longer now, there have been some changes to how mechanics work due to my progress, so please take this review as a sub 10 hour experience and nothing more.  [h1] This game ticks so many boxes for me. [/h1]  [h2] The good stuff [/h2]  [h3] Great game feel [/h3]  Walking, running, jumping, gliding, swinging, gathering, terraforming and fluidity of combat all feel really solid and play major roles in the world in their own unique way  [h3] Fun Exploration [/h3]  it has enough different meaningful encounters that you want to see what's upstairs in that derelict building, or cave that seemingly goes on forever. Usually when you go out of your way to explore, you are rewarded.  [h3] Seamless and interesting Questing system [/h3]  Quests aren't slow or meaningless. You're trying to find your next follower who have their own back stories to follow, or you can just happen to stumble upon a letter left by a [spoiler] mysterious princess in some shabby abandoned camp [/spoiler] which lead to scandals and secrets later on in your play through.  [h3] Less frustrating food and drink system [/h3]  You don't get hungry or thirsty, yet you can eat and drink. Why? Because they act as buffs! It's the best of both worlds because it's not a system you have to micro manage, yet if you use it, similar to potions, you will have an easier time, and it's totally your choice!  [h3] Clear map [/h3]  It's so easy to know what you need to do, and where you need to do it. You can place custom way points and uncover the fog of war system as you explore, it's so easy and intuitive. There are also teleport systems you can find (and ones you can build too) to make traversing the world much easier.  [h3] Upgrading weapons [/h3]  Really fun and easy upgrade system that lets you sacrifice weapons you find in the world for tokens which can be used to upgrade your favourite weapons to make them even more powerful. There are also other ways to get these tokens too.  [h2] The things i didn't like so much [/h2]  [h3] Building [/h3]  The game doesn't require you to build crazy things if you don't want too (I'm thinking like a big fortress to keep out waves of enemies like in Valheim or The Forest) Which is a good thing in my opinion. Building is fairly solid and easy to grasp, and someone with an imaginative brain could certainly create some wonders, however i found the UI for it a bit finicky. It stood out because it didn't feel as smooth as the rest of the game does.  [h3] Crafting [/h3]  I like the items you can craft, and the fact that it's pretty easy to craft stuff in general, but i HATE the fact you need to jump around from the work bench to one of the followers, or tab across to the basic stuff. I would like to see this reworked in a way that all the craftable items you have unlocked are available from the workbench. Do this and you have streamlined this process for us!  [h3] The red stuff [/h3]  Oh my god what a horrible awful frustrating mechanic!!!! GET RID OF THIS OR NERF IT PLEASE! you'll be walking jump and hopping over terrain to get somewhere and there is just this pit of death you couldn't see that kills you within 2 seconds. and most of the time you can't scamper up the edges to save yourself. You lose some of your items (Which is ok), however when you go to retrieve them, they have spawned on the side of the slippery terrain you can't properly scamper across to collect it! My suggestion with this, is make sure all the banks surrounding the red stuff are climbable, and increase the time you can be in there to give the player a fighting chance to recover from their mistake.,and also make the items that drop from you reachable 100% of the time.  [b] As an early access game this is a solid 9/10! There are some bits i would like to see changed in full release for it to keep this rating, but i have a lot of faith in the devs from what I've seen so far. I'm going to continue playing and unlock everything i can. I'm very excited to see where this title goes. [/b]

text: A dream game for anyone who loves both Minecraft and Terraria. It combines Terraria's epic fantasy world design with a building system that gives you far more freedom than Minecraft. You're not limited to simple blocks, you can customize structures piece by piece and build almost anything you can imagine.  The gameplay loop can get repetitive after a while: explore a new region, gather resources, craft better gear, and repeat. Playing with friends helps a lot and makes the grind much more enjoyable.  My only real complaint is the optimization. Despite being able to run games like Crimson Desert, Black Myth: Wukong, and Expedition 33 at a stable 60 FPS, Enshrouded struggles to maintain 60 FPS even on the lowest settings with upscaling enabled. Hopefully this gets improved before full release, since the game is still in Early Access.  Overall, it's a fantastic survival-crafting game with one of the best building systems out there.

text: This is a fantastic game for a group of friends! It's easy to pick up, there's lots to explore and do and it's been a blast!  But on the other hand, I feel like I spend more time compiling shaders than playing the game. Every tiny little update, I have to compile more shaders. It's fine if it's just a little bit, but in my experience, it fairly regularly breaks the shader cache and the game becomes an uplayable mess until I manually force all shaders to recompile, which is a 30 minute ordeal... No other game I play has shader compilation times this atrocious.  I was lenient before because it's early access, but the game is nearing a 2026 release and there are still too many game breaking issues. On top of the shader caching issue, building is inconsistent. There is a very specific speed at which you can build (about 140bpm), and any faster will cause missed inputs, gaps in the building, ghost blocks, etc. Worse, sometimes your building "cursor" is inaccurate. You place/break a block, and something else happens instead. Where did you just place/break that block? Who knows... At least you can undo with a keypress... Then the frequent ghost blocks if you try to place too fast, or if the cursor becomes broken... It's frustrating and frankly unacceptable for a game where building is a big selling point.  Another huge big issue I noticed is that a ton of various props in the game aren't obtainable by players. I acquired a free house through certainly legal means, but I cannot fix the windows because these specific windows cannot be obtained. Or the little decorative rock pillars. Or the other windows. Or the tarpaulin covers. Or the other little decorative rock pieces. Or these. Or that. It's everywhere. If you see something in a building game, you should be able to recreate it.  Finally, a few of the boss fights are just plain bad. I don't know how else to say it. The fell dragon youngling at the top of the mountain is the worst boss fight I've ever played. It just flies around forever so I can't hit it. The little hint says to bring stun arrows to knock it down. Okay, but why does it take a million stun arrows to knock it down once? Yes, it's a big dragon, but I built for melee. Give me a way to fight it... When you're lucky and it does the little spin move with fireballs thrown everywhere, you can parry them back, but half the time the dragon just flies away and you miss. The other half of the time, the dragon refuses to even do that move, giving you zero opportunity to hit it without a ranged weapon.  The best part is, once you finally knock it out of the sky and run over to fight it, it's on the other side of the ring from you and you spend an hour running over. And even if it lands by you, the dragon spawns in a bunch of these obnoxious wyverns to knock you around while you try to take your well deserved reward of an attack window... text: 400 hours played — and I’m still not bored. That should tell you everything.  This is easily one of the best survival RPGs released in years. Enshrouded doesn’t just give you systems — it gives you a world that genuinely pulls you in. The atmosphere is incredible. Exploring Embervale, especially inside the Shroud, feels tense and immersive. The vertical exploration with climbing and gliding makes discovery addictive. You constantly find hidden ruins, caves, and secrets that actually feel rewarding.  The building system is on another level. The voxel tools allow serious creativity — castles, villages, underground bases — you’re not fighting the mechanics, you’re building what you imagine. It’s one of the strongest building systems in the genre.  Combat feels solid and satisfying. Melee, ranged, and especially magic builds are fun and viable. The skill tree allows real specialization instead of just minor stat boosts. Boss fights feel earned.  Is it perfect? No — it’s Early Access, so there are minor balance quirks and occasional performance hiccups. But the foundation is extremely strong, and the developers clearly care.  The gameplay loop is dangerous: Explore → Loot → Build → Upgrade → Repeat …and suddenly it’s 3AM.  If a game keeps you hooked after 400 hours, that’s not hype — that’s quality.  Highly recommended.

text: You ever see a new cereal on the shelf you think "hey that looks good" then you grab it, try it, and its exactly what you expected? No more, no less, just "yeah that's good". That is this game. Its exactly what it says in the description, no more, no less, and its just fine. Everything you expect, you get, with all the quirks and weirdness and proprietary engine funsies, its just good. As a whole though, this game is as close to what I would vaguely consider a "Third-Person Terraria" as one could get. Which is huge praise because Terraria is singularly one of the greatest games in history, so to even mention it in this review says a lot. Early access as of the 0.8 update is fantastic. It takes some getting used to, but man when you get into it you GET INTO IT.

text: Mid to Late game crafting timers are way too long, It takes 40 minutes real life minutes (This varies, some crafts are longer) to craft enough materials to make stuff, without any way to speed it up (Sleeping through night doesn't speed up crafts as an example), let alone how long it takes to acquire food that temporarily increases your stats, food buffs are very important in this game.  It's at the point to where I idle with this game open and just play a second game on the side while waiting out craft timers, because the craft timers are that long, craft timers that are this extreme should never be a mechanic in any game, this game wastes the players time, I would refund it if I could but unfortunately, it takes a good few hours into the game till you reach these extreme timers that make the game very hard to want to play.

text: Based on Enshrouded (v0.7.2, incl. Melodies of the Mire) in solo gameplay as tank/warrior for 230 hours with most quests of this version completed.  [h1]TL;DR? [/h1] Even though I am usually very suspicious of early access games, I was hooked after playing the demo and then got a very positive surprise after buying Enshrouded. The game is looking stunning and – if you are into base building – is extremely fun and addictive. The limit is your imagination (well, and the range of you Flame Altars). The game is running stable. I would note some deduction in the “style scores” for the (lack of) variety in combat and dungeons, but I definitely got the bang for my buck already now!  [h1] What is it and what not? [/h1] I would describe Enshrouded as a base building game with questing. That may be simplified, but the main objective of the quests is to unlock new crafting stations and material to build and improve your base, providing the required stamina buffs for exploration and fights. Or to get weapons and armors. It is not a survival game where the player needs manage hunger, thirst, health, or hypothermia. The lore – except for the eponymous shroud – is less prominent and mainly told through notes and books. The game has different biomes ranging from light-filled meadows over dark forests to deserts and swampy jungles added in the latest update. All are visually stunning and providing an individual atmosphere. Each biome has a different range in difficulty level (not adapting to the players). This is true also for The Shroud – foggy, mold covered areas with a time limit to stay in these areas for the player character.   [h1]Role playing, combat, exploring[/h1] Character development and combat support playing the classical three main archetypes of warrior, thief, and mage – or any mix of them. The perk trees can be progressed individually and provide perks/perk trees for improving survival. You can also completely reset you perks and re-assign them, so there are no issues with later finding you got something wrong. Progress is gained by adventuring and crafting, not by using specific skills. Perks primarily affects you offense and defense, as there are no friendly or neutral NPCs to interact with (yet?).  I only played a tank/warrior (with a bow/wand to down those enemies that are otherwise unreachable) with a very direct approach. This is well balanced also in a solo play from my point of view. If you are approaching high level areas and getting swarmed it may be better to return later. The enemy variety is ok, even though once you know the pattern, the procedure in the fight gets very predictable (from either just a bit easier in areas or your level to outright a “loot farming exercise” in lower level areas).   [b]Exploration[/b] to me had a lesser aspect. Usually it is much easier to fly in with you glider as finding the right path to your target. Without any roads on the map this can be tedious. Indications that the objective is above or below don’t really help then. With the distribution of discoverable fast travel points (Ancient Spires) across the map, the possibility to set a limited amount of own bases (Flame Altars), and the glider to zip around, traversing the map is pretty straight forward. Dungeons – beside fighting enemies – often require to solve puzzles and platforming passages. Both are manageable (just not my cup of tea). You get used to the trap and puzzle types pretty quickly as they are repetitive.  [h1]Base Building and the Looks [/h1] Disclaimer: my rig is not exactly a potato (i9-10980XE/128GB/RTX 3080Ti 12GB, 1440p/2TB SSD) and I am playing on max settings for graphics.  The voxel based environment is extremely beautiful and atmospheric. The terrain blending smoothly, the lighting is gorgeous, and the sound is great to me (but I am a visual person, not an audiophile). The only thing that I feel is still a bit underwhelming is the variety of options currently available in the character editor and the cartoonish look of main NPCs (or “human crafting stations”).  However, [b]Base Building[/b] is where the game really shines for me. With the possibilities to choose from quite a range of materials and the ability to freely set every element or quickly build with some predefined base tiles that can be adapted, there is a fantastic variety in building you own home. Materials also have different visual representations, so roofs result in smooth are angled surfaces and not blocky stairs. Same is for the terrain which can be chopped away or added with different materials such as different stone types, dirt (grass), and sand. Even luminescent materials in different colors exist. This is complemented by furniture and clutter to make you base a home. I tried from a hill castle (of cause) to small villages and even caves. The limit is really the range of the Flame Altar, but that can be easily mitigated by using multiple.   [h1]Technical[/h1] The game ran solid with no crashes experienced. Load times are usually fast for starting the game (though I have occasions where it does some pre-processing for several minutes) as well as fast traveling. The controls work well – I am using keyboard and mouse. Timing your strikes and block is more important – just spamming the keyboard won’t get you far.  Up to now I only experienced one visual glitch (shroud spilling into my base and molded my strawberries, yikes) but that is already fixed. Other than that I only got stuck on one or two occasions (and needed to teleport back out) and had one “out of map experience” (glitching thought terrain and returned to the previous spawn points).  No complaints on stability or performance (I wish Bethesda games would run that smooth).  Looking forward to further development progress of this fantastic game.

text: (Early-mid game review) It's alright.  Like. Aggressively alright.  There's nothing that really makes me mad about its design. Nothing that really makes me feel strongly for or against the game. I guess my biggest complaint is that the character models are horribly ugly, but that's subjective and not really a valid criticism. The game feels exceptionally inoffensive in its design and direction. It's a crafting survival game more like Conan Exiles than something more sandbox focused like rust, minecraft or hell, even valheim. There is a progression path leading you forward, NPCs with tidbits of info to help keep you directed. It feels more structured than a true sandbox where unlockables feel deeply integrated into the progression, mandatory even.  The world is fun enough to explore, terrain manipulation letting you be cheesy is always a joy.  Combat is floaty and kinda junk. Skill tree seems good so far.  It's... Alright.  The game excels in vibes more than anything. The graphics, lighting and art style give it an almost fairy tale feel that is an absolute delight. The shroud zones are appropriately ominous feeling, especially early game. Building homes is genuinely comfy and cozy, even if the building controls are a little ass. Seeing everything come together and basically creating your own little village is great.  It's not bad by any means, I'd say it's pretty good. It's [b]aggressively[/b] alright. It'll scratch the craft/survival itch if you got it. It's just missing a little... Something. Something to make me want to log in and eagerly keep exploring/building.

text: This is a fun, Valheim like survival/adventure game (no eating/drinking to stay alive, you just get buffs) with a whole lot of potential. Personally if you are not to sure about this game just wait for the purchase, but I have been waiting for a game just like this one for a while and I have certainly been enjoying it.  The multiplayer gets too much hate, this is not a game meant for random people and I don't know why people are pretending it is. With 1-2 friends that are coordinated and don't rush quests there is not issue. If you want to play with more than a few people then issues might arise, but once again just don't rush quests alone.  The combat is fun, much more fun than Valhiem's, but still needs a bit more variety. I have by no means fought every enemy but most are pretty similar and not too difficult. The skill tree is fine, not to complicated (maybe a bit basic).  The building is more enjoyable than Valhiem's with much more customizability and depth. The only issues with space (you have a limited area to build than can be moved around) I could think of, is once again when you have too many people playing. The world reverting is a bit odd, but it keep the resources from being a super long grind (like Valhiem's). I think that chests shouldn't respawn, instead everyone on the server should have personal chests but it's not too much of an issue. text: Sharing some of my nitpicks i had with the game & positive feelings. Overall it's a good game. Farming:  - Make rare resources common and food buffs goes BRRRRRRRR - Pressing E A LOT OF TIMES.(There isn't an automated option as of yet)  - You can automated the watering-irrigation system and that's a PLUS  Barn/animals: - Some are cute( & you can pet them) - Getting 2 or more they can have babies - Good resources - AI path is dogshi, i left food for my goats in 10 spots, with 2k food portions available, of my 10 goats 6 ate from their bowls and 4 refused to eat, I bothered to google it and it's a bug... therefore this needs to be addressed.   - I feel like the rabbits/hares should produce something, they never produced anything, as of yet they're mostly cosmetic  Coop features I feel like we should have more options for coop settings, for example if I open my world for a stranger to get into it, either I allow them to edit the bases and have access to storage or I don't allow them to be able to have a storage and this results into them have limited freedom into the world outside of combat/mining etc...   Combat: It feels coop oriented or archer wise etc, playing as mage is powerful but some enemies pisses me off cause they're outside of range of wands, and their attack window doesn't allow usage of staff spells, aka making wizard slighty bad to play SP, however wizard has some really cool skills such as Radiant Aura and i wish we had more styles of Aura magics for different enemies than the Fell Faction.  If not playing with Wizard and instead you customize around archer-warrior or different styles of hybrid builds, you can have a fun build, as the game provides with tons of skills points as you progress, enabling you to customize your style of gameplay.   Experience  You get doing quests(its whatever), scrolls( doesnt even show up the amount you get..), mining(most efficient one), combat and if playing with radiant aura, Killing the Fell is the best method to XP farm.  I believe, if we got XP from farming, cutting trees, fishing etc. Would feel more immersive/natural  as progression than instead of only mining and killing stuff.  Summarizing :  I think as it's EA title, it needs more polishing, but it's a fun experience, specially if playing with you friends. If some of the issues are addressed properly it will be a major game for people to enjoy for years to come, that's for sure

text: Enshrouded has been an absolute joy to play. The building mechanics are easily some of the best in the genre, intuitive, flexible, and genuinely really fun to experiment with. I enjoy how the world feels like one giant co-op experience, making exploration and progression feel shared and meaningful among the whole group.  Crafting is done very well, and the game is packed with thoughtful QoL features. Magic chests that pull resources from anywhere in your base are a huge win for me, especially in a genre where item management can be a nightmare. Enshrouded handles inventory and materials far better than most survival games.  Exploration is another standout. The world is full of landmarks, areas and interesting things to discover. With each altar upgrade it opens up more of the shroud and creates a great sense of progression and pacing. Character progression is equally strong, the skill tree is simple, clean, and satisfying without being overwhelming.  Overall, Enshrouded is incredibly easy to understand, well paced, and polished, with a lot of care poured into its systems. Highly recommended for players of survival, building, and co-op exploration.

text: Not a bad open-world survival game. However, I have a lot of questions for the developers. The graphics are nice, but there is no optimization. Points of interest on the map can easily be missed because they are underground, and if you just run past the entrance, they won't even show up on your map, the obelisks don't reveal everything either. Why constantly mess with the balance in a single-player/co-op game? Magic used to be interesting and fun to play; there were only a couple of weak skills. But now they’ve "balanced" it to the point where only a few viable skills are left, while the rest are mediocre or straight-up trash. Melee weapons have a ton of downsides. It’s unclear how or when skills trigger—some don't make sense at all because what's written in the description only works half the time. It's also unclear how to increase your damage, since a two-handed sword, for instance, heavily falls behind dual blades in terms of DPS. They removed the uniqueness of armor crafting. Now it’s completely useless because you can find legendary-quality craftable gear in chests and from mobs, while you can only craft rare tier at best. Also, gems—what's the point? 95% of them are useless and require a ton of grinding, and the remaining 5% that are actually useful require specific conditions to even work. The map expansion is interesting, though. But why add Shroud damage if most enemies are immune to it? Just to bloat the loot pool in chests? And why so many survivors/NPCs? You can't give them any tasks, you just waste time building houses for them. Verdict: The game is interesting until about the halfway point, then it starts to feel like a tedious grind. There are too many dumb decisions that I disagree with, which actually worked much better before the official release. 7/10

text: Coming from a VERY beginner level gamer I have to say that I absolutely LOVE the customization that is allowed wiithin the settings, and the entire gaming experience along with it. What I mean is, my oldest son and my boyfriend are very experienced gamers and they WANT excitement, action, quests, skill-trees -the whole 9 yards! Oh, you can also adjust (in settings) how long it is day & night and other survival/game-play experience aspects as well. 10/10 recommend.

text: The ONLY negative thing I have to say about this game is that while it is technically "multi-player", the game runs so poorly in multi-player as to basically not work for anyone but the hose. That said, if you want to play a really good single player game, then read on.   Imagine a game with minecraft's ability to "dig a hole", because you feel like it. Having trouble climbing a mountain? No problem, just did a path into the rock face!   There are lots of hidden gems scattered around. No part of the map feels "empty" that I've found. Found a graveyard, and one of the graves looks freshly dug? Bust out the ol' pickaxe and find you some treasure! See a path that is obstructed by a giant pile of rubble? We've got explosive arrows to dig a hole straight through it!  This game has farming, base building, voxel manipulation to get things JUST-so, and more decorations than a Vanity fair meagazine.   I ventured to the end of the map and met a great "red wall", ominous and angular. I stepped beyond the barrier and was met with a feeling, almost like a message from beyond my sight; "You have reached the end of the early access area. Turn back now."  I stepped back and the sense of impending doom faded rapidly, but was quickly replaced with a thought, "This is early access?"  There are some minors bugs like the controls getting stuck in one direction (which can be easily fixed by opening the ESC menu and closing it), but overall this game feels very fleshed out. The amount of variety in the weapons and armor is pretty large.   The combat feels pretty good too, and I've learned some interesting tactics over this last week that I've played it. For instance, bats are annoying, but burst of light grounds them temporarily!  I've hit the level cap of 35 (it was not easy on my difficulty level), and I'm eager for more content to be released.   If you like games like Fable, Minecraft, Stardew Valley, you'll probably get a kick out of this.

text: So as a foreword: I absolutely despise crafting+survival games. Like to the point of actively avoiding them.  Foreword over. THAT SAID, when my buddy suggested Enshrouded as our new game to get horribly addicted to, I had one caveat to trying it: I wanted absolutely zero part in the base building. No hate for those that like it, I'm just not super-creative in this aspect, and don't wanna shape our base at all. He does the building, I do the fighting. What could go wrong?  Turns out, nothing! The combat is rock solid. Fast-paced, hard-scaling (especially once you have gliders, hoooo boy) and the grind ain't so bad. Hell, I even started somewhat learning the whole crafting system because I made a Ranger...which requires making your ammo.  In conclusion: absolutely solid game, has me chomping at the bit for the next major update. My only criticism:  PLEASE make crafting arrows slightly less tedious. The number of times I've said "hold on I gotta go on a MAGICAL JOURNEY to scrounge up some twigs" is insanely high. Like I'm not even asking for a significant buff, maybe either make twigs drop at 2x rate (as most things only harvest to 1x twig) or reduce the craft requirement for arrows to 5x twigs in recipe.  In conclusion: - base building: seems decent, although have someone carrying a torch near you for super deep caves. Idk I did no part of this.  - combat: awesome, super fun, shoot things in the face for more damage or just auto-fire and it'll soft-lock a target for you if you're getting ganged up on.  - ammo requirements: "I'M OUT OF ARROWS GIMME TEN MINUTES"  - crafting: it's ok. I kinda like cooking despite it being "get meat, shove in fire" because my dingus friend keeps refusing to eat and buff his health bar before we do Halls lmao. Like eat your lunchable dude, it'll help.

text: Great Survival Game / Base Building.   Here's what the game needs before 1.0:  - Melee Combat Improvement   Melee combat is wayyyyy too basic. Please just add a heavy attack at the very least.  I find myself having to just spam left click and it's super boring. The parry doesn't really feel rewarding. It needs a better animation. Something more dramatic. Magic/Spells: Same thing here, better animations + cooler or more spells. If there are better spells ill have to see later but even the fireball spell is just a small fire projectile that does aoe. Feels a bit weird. Chain lightning is fine , ice bolt ok, but feels like staff spells overall besides maybe the healing spells are bit basic and lack variety. Maybe add things like idk frost tornadoes and fire rain, things like that.   Another thing on this. Not being able to move while casting staff spells or even shooting the bow feels terrible. text: So... I've never really been a fan of survival type games, I'm more an MMO kinda girl, but I have been enjoying this and am looking forward to where the game has to go.  The whole camp building thing is really kinda cool from some of the images I have seen of other players' plots (homes) and I have dabbled a VERY little so far. text: I am writing this review during Early Access shortly after the "Thralls of the Twilight" update, so keep that in mind when reading this.  Enshrouded is a game with a HUGE world that keeps you playing for hours. It is so big that you could spend hours of gameplay just walking to explore the map if it weren't for the gliders and grappling hooks the game allows you to use as transportation. After spending hours exploring, looting, and fighting, I thought I had explored a quarter of the map, but I was so, so wrong. There are many areas and terrains to experience and quests to unlock through lore hidden among the Shroud and Embervale.   The crafting system is fairly similar to many survival crafting games, with the premise being: kill/loot, bring to crafting bench or special crafting station, and create/queue the item to craft. You can easily spend hours to days gathering and building while upgrading your character's equipment and armor, but thanks to the use of server settings you can adjust the amount of resources gained, enemy density, and experience gained to tailor your gameplay to your desires.   Beyond the resource grinds and quests, you can find yourself creating villages for the NPC's you will find along the way as a sort of palette cleanser from the monotony of grinding. The building is simple and could use some more shape variation IMO, something similar to that of 7DTD's system. The settlement building is a great way to bring your creative side out and leave your own mark on Embervale.   Overall, the game is wonderful and perfect for hopping on and off with or without friends to splurge on some free hours. I would recommend this game to friends as a 9/10 game, even in early access, with my only major gripe/want from the developers is to PLEASE ADD WRITABLE TEXT SIGNS and NAMEABLE LOCATION MARKERS. I find it very hard to keep track of what is in each of my chests when organizing and losing track of what resource I have saved on the map.   Thank you, Keen Games, for the hard work and dedication.

text: I am amazed how much substance/content Enshrouded has to offer even in early access, especially compared to the other survival games I've played so far.   It feels more like playing Skyrim or Breath of the Wild than mindlessly grinding for resources like in Dune: Awakening e.g. There is [b]SO[/b] much to discover everywhere, beautifully handcrafted, interesting and sometimes challenging locations and not just copypasta filling the map with the same stuff over and over again.  The talent tree is really good, so is fighting and the available build diversity. Especially bow and dagger combat are so much fun once you got a working build. We are playing in a group of 3, with a mage/healer and a figher/tank and it feels more like a rpg, than a survival game.  Graphics are really good, even if the characters don't look too hot. I'd really wish they would redo the character models and give way more options in the character creator. Music is fitting, sound is okish, nothing too special in this department.   --> Doesn't feel like an early access game and more like a single player rpg that you can play with friends. If you are into survival games, you should definitively give this one a try. Thank you devs, awesome game!

text: I have been playing video games for 35 years, this is one of the best games I have played. You can tell the dev team put their heart and soul into this game. To address negative reviews , rewarding games come at the cost of actual limitations and challenges. For one you can adjust the difficulty in depth in the settings its very easy to make this game a breeze or difficult. Would a mount be nice sure but so would you being able to read a basic terrain map to optimize your flight paths. Put a teleporter at the highest point in a biome and glide to your destination with ease. Put points into skills that make stamina less of an issue they give you the tools use them. On to the important stuff , an incredibly in depth building system. Fun missions and bosses, great combat and mechanics. This game is absolutely gorgeous without needing insane specs to run it well. Puzzles that make you sweat along with obstacles. They have steadily made this game better and better I have full faith in this team. Only things I would like to see, more glowing armor and weapons I love them lol. Have gems do more than what they do currently they are very under powered. Higher level cap for progression and it would be awesome to have a spell sword type tree. All in all if I can get 340 hours of fun from 30 bucks you are more than getting your moneys worth.

text: Let me say right off that I love the game. I have had it for three weeks and have 225 hrs of play. It's fun to play, runs great, 225 hrs and not one crash or freeze or any other tech issues to speak of. I have noticed that the further along in the game I progressed I started noticing a few glitches here and there but nothing game breaking. It's an early access game but plays like a finished product. Huge map area and lots of content for early access. One thing I should stress for people interested in this game because of it being tagged as a survival game, IT IS NOT a survival game. It is a RPG with crafting and exploration. You do not have to do any of the things you need to do to survive such as eat, drink, sleep, treat wounds and illness, or battle exposure or fatigue. So if you're looking for that type of game look elswhere. Now, as much as I like the game, there are a few things I wish were different and that I hope the devs improve upon as it progresses. The building mechanics are pretty good. while you can build anywhere you are restricted by the fact that you can only rotate items 90 degrees so everything must be placed at right angles of each other. Would like to have ability for full 360 degree rotation of placeable objects. I place a lot of importance on character customization which this game has but could have a few more choices. Would like to see some more height, body type, hair and facial feature choices etc. Again, it's early access, so hopefully more choices will be coming. This game has very little interaction with NPC's. All NPC's are enemies except for a few that are basically just quest givers and crafting sources. Would love to have some non-combative NPC's you could encounter on your journeys. I should say that I have only played solo and perhaps the interaction with NPC's is not needed so much during co-op play. While I feel there is a lot they can do to improve some of the mechanics and immersion of the game I really enjoy playing it and definitely recommend it for people who like to explore, craft, and build.

text: I've been completely absorbed in Enshrouded's vast world, and I'm loving every minute of it! This early access game has blown me away with its stunning visuals, immersive gameplay, and creative freedom.  What Works Well:  Building Mechanics: The building system is incredibly intuitive and flexible, allowing me to craft amazing bases that are both functional and visually appealing, from a necromancer lair hidden in the mountain, or a majestic castle in the middle of the forest.  Exploration: The world of Embervale is breathtakingly beautiful, featuring a perfect blend of realistic and fantastical elements. I love discovering hidden secrets and scenic views, or just gliding my way above a red shrouded area.   Combat: The combat mechanics are both engaging and challenging, but playing as melee can be a bit boring compared to archer and magic (Hope they will improve the parry mechanic at least). Teaming up with friends makes the game even more enjoyable, especially when each team knows their role. Be it building a town or simply clearing a dungeon.  What needs work:  Game performance: It's terrible. Realy. I know it's an early access game, just want to point it out anyway. It's very demanding despite not being a really good graphic.  Overall Experience: Enshrouded has exceeded my expectations, offering a sense of freedom and creativity with its masterful blend of survival, crafting, and action RPG elements. This game is a must-play for fans of fantasy survival games.

text: I picked up Enshrouded last week with a friend, and honestly, I didn’t expect to fall this hard for a game so fast. The world is absolutely beautiful and haunting at the same time—exploring the valleys, ruins, and hidden corners feels like stepping into a living fantasy painting. The survival and building systems feel intuitive but deep enough to stay interesting, and uncovering new gear makes every adventure feel rewarding.  Co-op is where this game truly shines. My friend and I have spent hours building, fighting, and wandering—sometimes with a real plan, sometimes just “let’s see what’s over that hill” vibes. Either way, it’s always fun.  And now I’m so hyped for Update 7. The water update looks gorgeous and adds exactly the kind of atmosphere and immersion the world has been teasing since day one. Seeing the devs continue to expand and refine things just makes me more confident that this game is only going to get better with time.  If you love exploration, building, and a world you can genuinely get lost in—this one’s for you.

Hopefully they rework melee combat before the game leaves EA, but there are more than enough extremely well done game mechanics to overshadow the dated combat.

text: [b]Wasted potential.[/b]  After some great initial impressions the game quickly turns into a sluggish grindfest. Performance needs to be improved, combat is clunky, classes are unbalanced, enemy variety is a joke, and the default difficulty feels like it was made up by a malnourished, sleep deprived redditor.  To its credit, the game looks gorgeous; building and chilling in your base crafting stuff is a vibe, and the world settings are highly customizable so if the difficulty makes you frantically look for your fent dealer's contact info for another hit just so you can tolerate it, you can simply crank that stuff way down and relax...  HOWEVER, you really need to turn your brain off to be able to enjoy this game after you've left the first biome. You'll come to realize quite fast that you're fighting the same enemies over and over again, while dealing with the same annoying mechanics and debuffs, grinding the same handful of resources just so you can craft a piece of gear that feels like you've done an endgame MMO raid and received a green item 5 levels below the raid's requirements, and then moving on to the next biome, rinse and repeat. And that's the entire game. A mindboggling grind on a progression treadmill that barely rewards you with anything. And don't even get me started on how I'm lvl 31 slinging fireballs at lvl 21 flying squids that gigazap me into my grave in 3 shots unless I chug 6 potions and 2 energy drinks to regain my mana that disappears before I get to the second syllable of wingardium leviosa; gulp down a restaurant's entire menu and unlock my jaw to swallow the line cook whole for that sweet 50 hp bonus; switch to my wand to blow up the projectiles, dodge forward 6, maybe 7 times to avoid the swarm of bugs, all for that sweet, sweet loot of 4 goo that lets me finally craft a pair of soggy lvl 18 socks. Yeah, yeah I know, "Skill issue, take the L unc".  TLDR: Enshrouded is more frustrating than fun. I hope the devs continue to improve the game in early access and listen to criticism, and I hope I can change my review to a thumbs up in the future. But as it stands, I would not recommend the game.

And don't even get me started on how I'm lvl 31 slinging fireballs at lvl 21 flying squids that gigazap me into my grave in 3 shots unless I chug 6 potions and 2 energy drinks to regain my mana that disappears before I get to the second syllable of wingardium leviosa; gulp down a restaurant's entire menu and unlock my jaw to swallow the line cook whole for that sweet 50 hp bonus; switch to my wand to blow up the projectiles, dodge forward 6, maybe 7 times to avoid the swarm of bugs, all for that sweet, sweet loot of 4 goo that lets me finally craft a pair of soggy lvl 18 socks. Yeah, yeah I know, "Skill issue, take the L unc".  TLDR: Enshrouded is more frustrating than fun. I hope the devs continue to improve the game in early access and listen to criticism, and I hope I can change my review to a thumbs up in the future. But as it stands, I would not recommend the game.

text: I have really been enjoying this game quite a bit and actually taking my time with it. The Lighting and shadows are fantastic, very realistic.  Gliders and grappling hooks rock. Exploration is key to advancing and being able to build/craft new items.  Combat can be alot of fun. I personally have an Nvidia 2070 RTX (not the super), on Ultra graphics settings, and this game runs amazingly smooth, no jittering, no lag, no frame rate drop and I have not had a single crash in 84 hours.  Simple truth.   The iffy?  (it's early access so I won't say bad)  Player characters could use ALOT more customization and could be able to sit in chairs at least?  Seriously what good is a chair if you can't sit in it? Also.. maybe the ability to choose to identify as tall? What's a hobbit without their tall wizard friend? a dead hobbit.   Some of the armor..  Helmets specifically, look like .. like when you were a kid and your mom, who has not a creative bone in her body, wanted to save money on your Halloween costume and made it herself and now you have no choice but to wear it out of necessity in order to get your candy, no matter how horrible it looks. Seriously, they are that bad.  No weather, at all.  The NPC's talk about building them a house with a roof in order to take them out of the elements. What elements? Where are the elements? Why do you need a roof, it's always sunny, it never snows or rains or storms! It's the perfect weather all year long!   Lack of water on the map. Not lack of, there is not a single lake, pond, river or even a puddle. Where exactly is my water well getting it's water from? By the time I got the final few building blocks, I really lost the need to build anything at all, especially when buildings hardly have a function or purpose. Seriously, new additions/changes for the better to this game could make it fantastic!  UPDATE 532 HOURS LATER :    The devs are amazing and have pretty much rectified any cons I posted. text: I was hesitant to buy this game because of a handful of negative reviews, but I'm glad I went ahead and pulled the trigger on getting this game for myself and a +1 to play with. I highly recommend you have a separate character and world if you're going to be playing a lot solo and also with a friend, as you will want to make sure you both are relatively close in level, gear, quest progression, etc. when playing together.  Pros-  Incredibly beautiful, highly detailed world. I'm constantly amazed at the level of detail in each new little town and point of interest I discover. Even when running through random forests, you'll come across little details you know  Almost 100 hours in and have only explored maybe 75% of the map, it's huge. Hand-crafted world so no generic procedurally generated world with no soul. Wide range of playstyles to choose from with skill trees to further tailor to your play style. Easily the best building tools of any crafting game I've ever played. It'll ruin your experience building anything in your other popular survival crafting games. Well-balanced progression. If you take your time, there's a couple hundred hours of quality content to enjoy in your first playthrough. This game rewards and promotes you taking your time, but doesn't handcuff you to your skill level biomes, weapons, etc. but that said, you'll often find yourself too far progressed in some areas while other areas need more attention (ie high xp level but too low of flame altar level). Survivors, villagers, pets, etc add a really nice touch to make your home bases really come alive. For those of us that are sometimes a bit creatively impaired, it's so great discovering a little homestead or monastery, claiming the land, fixing it up, and customizing it to your liking. For the creatively gifted though, the options are endless. Gameplay and combat are a challenge for two people that aren't good at video games, and have a nice variety of enemy types and skill levels. Tons of customization for those that really want to curate their own difficulty. Not too much handholding. You'll have to figure out the puzzles and navigate makes on your own for the most part.  Cons- For some of y'all, no procedurally generated maps may be a negative for replayability. If you need thousands of hours playing time for you to feel like you got your money's worth, this game might not be for you, especially if you need to constantly be on the move. If you plan to enjoy the farming, cooking, building, customizing, decorating, etc, you should be able to hit a thousand hours if you're enjoying the first couple hundred. Dungeons can feel really painful to navigate. Some "find the things" dungeons can feel like straight up time-wasters and can feel painfully difficult for the sake of being difficult. Some areas and floors within dungeons can look completely identical, sometimes having you really confused on where you are, where you came from, and where you need to go to progress. Some can take more than a few hours to finish, which feels excessive to me. You'll often find yourself on your way to quests you can't access yet due to too low level of flame altar (different from char level) or spending a half hour trying to go around the wrong side of a mountain range, or you get to your quest location but realize you gotta run all the way the other direction again because you didn't take a mountain road or cave passage because it's at an inaccessible elevation. Resources can feel a little grind-y at times. You'll be spending way more time than expected just chopping down trees to make charcoal. Inventory space is way too limited for much of the game.  Overall, this game is great though. If you're on the fence, and you like these kinds of games, get it. You won't be disappointed.
